Mr. Speaker, My attention has been drawn to the statement that the Nationalist party of the province of Quebec is about to put candidates in the field on its own behalf against Liberal and Conservative candi-

dates, and I am told the suggestion is being made that there is some collusion between the Nationalist party of the province of Quebec and my government or the friends of my government in regard to this campaign of the Nationalist party. The suggestion is also made that because the friends of the present Government and the Nationalist party both opposed Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the election of 1911 that there is now some connection or collusion and that my supporters and friends are in fact encouraging the Nationalist party of Quebec in the course which they are adopting.
I desire to make a most emphatic, unreserved, and comprehensive denial of this statement. There is not and never will be any conection or collusion whatever between my friends and supporters and those of the Nationalist party of Quebec.
I regard the attitude of the Nationalist party of Quebec in this war as unpatriotic, and I consider that it is the first duty of myself- and my friends to assist in defeating that party and to prevent it, so far as we are able, from being in a position to exercise any political power in Canada,

subsubtopic: TELEGRAM FROM THE NON PARTISAN LEAGUE-STATEMENT BY SIR GEORGE FOSTER.
speechtext:
The hon.

member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) asked me a question yesterday and I replied to him that I would make a statement in the House as quickly as possible with reference to what was involved in the telegram which he read and the question which he put. I am obliged to do that in a little fuller way than simply an oral and categorical answer, in order to give the information which I think is necessary, and to give the status of the case in point.
The Non-Partisan League protest against the action of the Board of Grain Supervisors in fixing a maximum price of $2.40 for No. 1 Northern at Fort William and affirm that, as admission duty free to the United States, was made possible by Act of the Government, the advantage of the higher price in the United States should not be denied.
In normal times this position would be justifiable. But these are abnormal times and the conditions imposed by the war introduce and give force to. other considerations. The British and Allied Governments are in urgent need of supplies of wheat and are appealing to Canada and the United States for their total available surplus. That appeal is accentuated by the practical impossibility of readily getting supplies from Australia, India, and Argentina on account of the difficulties of transport. To carry supplies from Atlantic ports to "Great Britain and the Allies, ships have been diverted from Oriental, Australian, and Mediterranean services, and the Royal Wheat Commission are loading a large number of vessels simultaneously at Atlantic ports. An even flow of grain is necessary in order to prevent ruinous delay in the despatch of these vessels and to keep up the supply for the Allied needs.
Canada was therefore urgently pressed to forward for shipment all its surplus of the crop of 1916-17, for August delivery. This surplus was lying mainly in storage in the elevators and held for highest possible prices, and sales at greatly advanced offers were not forthcoming. The Board of Grain Supervisors, appointed to secure and facilitate the movement of this grain, faced this situation.
The United States Government had no authority for fixing prices on their side of the line pending the passage by Congress of necessary legislation, and any attempts by the Allies to purchase for present pressing needs would have unduly promoted speculative prices in that country. If no maximum price had been fixed in Canada,
the attempt to purchase for pressing August delivery would have sky-rocketted wheat prices, flour would have followed wheat and bread would have followed flour, and the Allies and all consumers in Canada would have suffered for the benefit of a limited number of holders of grain in store, bought at much lower prices.
The board herefore decided to fix what many considered the high price of $2.40 for No. 1 Northern at Fort William and to stop dealing in futures on the Exchange. That action has aided in securing the required supply of wheat for the Allies and has prevented a large speculative rise in wheat, which would have been closely followed by a corresponding increase in flour and bread-stuffs in Canada, which would have greatly enhanced the present high cost of living.
It appears to be a case in which the general and public interests of the vast majority must be considered paramount to the gaining by a few of a temporary higher speculative price. The board has not stopped the export of wheat by individual farmers, but has only required information of quantities and grades shipped.
The board has fixed no prices for the crop of 1917-18.
Now that the required legislation has been passed at Washington, and the Controller of Food Prices appointed, co-operation between the two countries may be expected to control and equalize the prices of wheat in both. The immediate effect of the completion of this legislation in the United States and the organization founded thereon has been to cause a rapid fall in wheat prices in that country, and to-day's transactions are below the fixed Canadian price.
As to the composition of the Board of Grain Supervisors, the Government gave the most careful consideration to that matter. The intricacies and the involved character of the business under supervision and the complex and widely extended mechanism connected therewith made it necessary to have some men intimately acquainted w.ith the trade as members of the board, and an endeavour was made to represent fairly the consuming and producing interests. Mr. Wood, as President of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, Mr. Rathwell, as a prominent farmer of Saskatchewan, and Mr. -Crerar, who is an influential member of the Grain Growers' Association, specially represent the producers' interest.
It is admitted that the fixing of a maximum price for wheat carries logically the-

regulation of the price of flour and other staple food products. These matters are now under consideration, and the completion of United States control legislation will render co-operation possible in the operations of the Canadian Food Controller.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every member of this House-for that matter every citizen of Canada-has the most profound sympathy with the Prime Minister and the members of the Administration who are charged with the responsibility of carrying on the Government during the greatest conflict of .all the 'ages, but, while our main purpose in Parliament must be to carry forward this war to a successful termination, nevertheless, side by side with that purpose there are large domestic problems which must be dealt with. The economic and financial stability of the country must be maintained, our production must be increased, and we must make every effort in our power to endeavour to at least maintain the credit of our country, and enable it to meet the demands that must be made upon it financially.
The largest domestic problem that must engage the attention of the people of this country is that connected with transportation. The war was not an inherited legacy of this Administration. It came since this Administration was called into existence, but the transportation problem, in its present acuteness, was the legacy that was inherited when this Government came into power in 1911. Any thoughtful man, reviewing the history of the past in this country, must be convinced of that fact, and my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) last night very properly put his

finger' mpon the weak spot of the legislation that has been passed in Canada during the past fifteen or twenty years. It serves no useful purpose, Mr. 'Speaker, to dwell upon the past. It serves no useful purpose to endeavour to allocate blame. It is a condition, and not a theory, that confronts this country. We have four systems of rail transportation. We have the Government system, the Grand Trunk system, the Canadian Northern system and the Canadian Pacific system. We cannot, by any thought or act change those facts as they exist. They are with us, and with them are the responsibilities arising out of the legislation that called them into being. There is just this that might be said on behalf of those of us who, in the years that are past, have suppoited Conservative policies and programmes:	that
there has not been placed upon the statute books of this country, by this Government, a single Act passed by this Parliament that has had to do with the initiation of any one of those enterprises. It is true this Government had something to do with respect to the enterprises to which I have referred, but the one enterprise that the Conservative Government must be responsible for is that system known as the C anadian Pacific 'railway. The other two enterprises were fathered by the Liberal party in their entirety, and that party must take .all the glory and blame that attach to such fatherhood. These are the facts, and it is idle at this time to discuss that question, and it serves no useful purpose to endeavour to blame one party or to approve of the action of the other party. I do not purpose to endeavour to review the legislation which has led up to the existing condition. We have spent millions of dollars in establishing terminals at Halifax, Fort William, St. John and Vancouver, and in providing rail facilities for the handling of traffic that we hope will one day come into being.
All this we have done in faith, faith being the evidence of things not seen and the substance of things hoped for. If at times our faith far outran any warrant that there might have been for it; if at times our optimism was somewhat stronger than that which our sense of cahtion should have induced, at least we recognize the fact: that we have provided transportation facilities in this country to meet the needs of a population at least three times greater than we now have. How to take care of that condition until the population of
7,500,000	shall have been expanded into 30,-
000,000 is a question that must receive careful consideration on the part, of every thoughtful man in this country.
It is an elementary rule of transportation that he who uses the transportation facilities should pay for them. It is a rule, of transportation that the man who travels or transports his freight or traffic should pay for that service. Unfortunately, however, the service provided far exceeds the demands made upon it and if the credit of the country is locked up behind the enterprises then the taxpayers as a whole must be called upon to pay that which, according to the principles, that govern transportation, should be paid only by those who use the facilities. That is the reason why the farmer of the West must continue for many years to pay directly for the upkeep of two transportation systems that do not earn sufficient money to meet the fixed charges upon their outstanding indebtedness. That is a fixed and definite charge which, because of the creating of facilities beyond the demands of the community, must be met by the taxation of all classes, rich and poor, the farmer and the artisan. That measure of taxation is large, and it is increasing. It is something that we must meet, in every sense of the term, frankly and honestly. There is no use glossing it over;, we must look it fairly in the eye.
I want to show to-day that the maintaining of the credit of the two roads to which I have referred involves a charge on the taxpayers of Canada of not less than $1,-
500,000	a month or $18,000,000 per annum. That enormous sum, which must be met by general taxes upon the people, should, according to every fixed rule governing transportation, be met only by those who use the facilities. It will not be. That means a direct tax upon the grain producer of the West; it means a direct tax upon the steel producer and the manufacturer of the East.	Moreover-I make this observation in passing-when, we placed wheat upon the free list and allowed it by reason of our Order in Council free access into the markets of the United States, at one stroke of the pen we increased the obligation that must be borne by the taxpayers of Canada as a whole. Why? Because last year the Canadian [Northern alone handled 138,000,000 bushels of wheat which it moved east. If my hon. friends opposite are correct in saying that wheat will move no longer east, but south, the revenues of these transportation companies will be lessened to the extent that the haul-

ing of that wheat east would earn. The result is an added tax upon the wheat producer-and I am not sure that he will not have to bear an added burden in the form of taxation to meet the deficit in connection with our transportation facilities to an amount equal to, if not exceeding, the benefits that will accrue to him by reason of the increased prices. That is an economic consideration that should be steadily kept in view in the discussion of matters affecting transportation.
I have in days past-in fact, at almost-every session since this Parliament met- discussed at some length the history of our transportation facilities. I shall not weary the House to-day by again going over that discussion. The condition that confronts the Government, this Parliament, and the people of this country, has arisen under the circumstances to which I have alluded. I should like to correct the false impression of the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) who indicated the other evening that the war had lessened the traffic of the railways. This war had added tremendously to. the revenues of the railways. When you look at the Trade and Commerce returns of Canada and observe that there has been a great expansion in our exports and a great increase in our imports, you will realize that the demands made upon our transportation facilities have accordingly increased. Hence it is that the operating revenues of the Canadian Pacific are larger this year than ever before in its history; that the operating revenues of the Canadian Northern are larger this year than ever before in its history. I regret, however, to say that last year the operating revenues of the Grand Trunk Pacific were less than the amount , of money received for hire of its equipment. The surplus equipment rented produced more net revenue last year to the Grand Trunk Pacific than its operating revenue. Perhaps its location had something to do with that. The two roads in question have operated, notwithstanding the conditions of trade and commerce in this country, at a loss. The net revenue of the Canadian Northern for the year ended June 30, 1917, was something like $11,500,000, but the fixed charges against its revenues-fixed charges for interest upon its bonds, for rental of properties leased, and for equipment- amounted to the very large sum of over $15,000,000. If you add to that the interest which is not added in the blue book submitted to the House-interest upon the $15,000,000 that was loaned by the people to that road and which absorbs an addi-

tional $900,000 per annum-you will observe that the total fixed charges of the road will amount to nearly $20,000,000 per annum. If you look at page 7 of the blue book you will find the statement that there is an annual interest charge of $14,405,643.13; to that is to be -added equipment obligations payable under the scheme by which a certain sum per annum of principal and interest is paid for equipment, absorbing a further sum of $3,735,000. $3,735,000 plus $14,405,000 makes $18,000,000, and to that is to be added the interest upon the loan referred to at page 11 of the blue book, $15,000,000 at six per cent per -annum, making $900,000 more. So that the total sum exceeds $19,000,000 of fixed charges to maintain that system when it is completed. In the meantime its capital is being depleted by the payment of interest out of the proceeds of bonds. The delay in the completion of construction is absorbing day by day large sums by way of interest beyond what was contemplated when the terminals, for instance, at Montreal were conceived. Just that much less money, therefore, is available for construction, and the burden that must be borne by the people is greater to that extent. This $20,000,000 in round figures is the sum per annum that the Canadian Northern must earn as a surplus out of its operations to meet its fixed charges. I am advised-my judgment may not be worth very much, but my estimate of the earnings of the system was, at least, more nearly correct than that made by the Third Vice-President of the Canadian Northern railway three years ago-that we cannot hope in less than five or seven years to' earn $20,000,000 of surplus in the operating of that road when it is completed, even under the very best conditions we can conceive of. $20,000,000 is a very large sum to earn by way of surplus. It means an operating revenue of nearer $80,000,000 than any other figure I can name, having regard to the newness of the system. A ratio of 100 to 25 as between gross earnings and operating expenses would not be unfair, having regard to the character of the system and the difficulties that must be experienced in the operation of a new venture.
Under these conditions, with this system in this condition, with its bonds guaranteed by the provinces and by the Dominion, with the guarantees underlying the fourth mortgage that we made in 1914, and with the additional obligation restmg upon this road by reason of the outstanding securities in England being treated as being partially

guaranteed by this country because of our fourth mortgage which ranks after those securities, we have to do one of three things, and there is, it seems to m , no getting away from that. We have to determine, first of all, whether or not we shall let that property go into the hands of a receiver, second, whether we shall give it financial aid, and third, whether we shall acquire the' road and the stock by one of three methods:
(a)	By negotiation, agreement and purchase;
(b)	By expropriation;
(e) By virtue of the Statute of 1914.
So far as the question of a receivership is concerned, the Drayton-Acworth report found against it; the Minister of Finance said that it was impossible to think of a receivership in this country at this time. For my part, I have never been afraid of this bogey of a receivership. I said in 1914 that if I had my own way (which I did not have, perhaps fortunately for this country), that road would have been put into the hands of a statutory receiver; Mackenzie and Mann would havie been replaced, and qualified receivers, appointed by this Parliament and subject to this Parliament, would have administered that property as a trust for the purpose of completing it, *when we could have determined what we should do with it. That was the course advocated by me at that time. A receivership need not be such a bogey as it appears to be in the minds of some persons; 75 per cent of all the roads in the United States have passed through the hands of receivers, and the result of a receivership could be only one thing: It would remove from the control of the property the Mackenzie and Mann interests; it would conserve it for the people whose money built it, and it would enable the people of Canada to acquire some first hand knowledge of the whole venture, which knowledge we do not yet possess. I am, however, in the position of one who is told by men who occupy official positions-and whose opinions, by virtue of their office, are entitled to a consideration that must be denied to mine

that a receivership cannot be thought of. Some hon. gentlemen opposite agree with that view; gentlemen who have held high office hold that view, and the best consensus of opinion on this side is the same. I wall, therefore, subordinate my opinion to theirs, and we shall dismiss the question of a receivership. But were I in a position of authority to-day, instead of the legislation which is now being submitted to the House, I would preserve
the identity of the Canadian Northern by the appointment of a statutory receiver or statutory receivers, occupying the position that Mackenzie and Mann occupy, and I would advance such moneys as might be necessary to place the undertaking on its feet as was done in the case of the Wabash, the Bock Island, and the Chicago Great Western railways, and, those receivers' certificates would have prior claim over the interest on the 4 per cent perpetual debenture stock of the Canadian Northern and over every other security except those guaranteed by the provinces and the Dominion. Fortunately, perhaps, for this country, I have no power, but no gentleman residing outside of Canada and occupying first-class business positions, positions of the very highest importance, see any difficulty in carrying that out as a business proposition. But it will not be done, so we will dismiss it from consideration.
As to the second point, namely, giving financial aid to this road, the Canadian people are not disposed to make further loans to Mackenzie and Mann. The consensus of opinion in this Parliament and outside of it is that we have lent all the money we should lend and made all the advances we should make to those gentlemen, and that the time has come when those with whose credit and money the road has been constructed, should have, at least, a dominant voice in its administration. We must remember that the men in charge of that corporation, whether we like them or dislike them, have control, in this country, of traffic facilities measuring 9,500 miles and are in charge of annual revenues of over $40,000,000. They are but trustees. It is admitted that, although they have given some time and attention to the financing of the road and that they have done that work admirably, they have no cash investment in it; and that being the case, they occupy the position of trustees of a great enterprise for the Canadian people. As they are unable to finance it, I submit that, if the collective credit of Canada must finance the enterprise, then the people of Canada must direct how that enterprise shall be completed; how its facilities shall be used; how the traffic shall be regulated, and what shall be the character of the service it shall give to the people who have financed it. I, therefore, without further elaboration, dismiss the question of additional financial aid to the road.
I pass on to the consideration of the third alternative that presents itself to' Government or to Parliament, and that is the acquisition of the property, whether it be the

physical property or the stock. There were open to the Government three methods by which they could acquire the road:
(a)	By agreement, negotiation and purchase;
(b)	By expropriation;
(c)	By the exercise of the powers conferred by Parliament upon the Government in 1914.
The Government have chosen (a) with a combination of (c). They purpose acquiring this property, or the shares that represent it, by negotiation, agreement and purchase, together with ;a submission to arbitration of the question as to what shall be paid for those shares and that property. 1 will not take up the time of the House at this moment to discuss the question of expropriation. It was open for this country to expropriate the property without reference to the statute of 1914 to which I shall presently refer. It is fair, however, to say that that method was eliminated. Let us now proceed to consider the other methods of acquiring the property. I take it that it is the common sense of Parliament that the property should be acquired; in fact, the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) contemplates an approval of the principle of the acquisition of the system. There is no doubt as to that, and my hon. friend very properly nods assent. We may, therefore, say that this House is a unit in assuming that we shall acquire control of the Canadian Northern system. That involves two questions:
1.	How shall that be done?
2.	How shall the price, if any, that .is to be paid, be determined?
I am not in accord with the Government's legislation upon the first point, and I shall show that, upon the isecond point, there must he very important amendments made or this country is going to suffer enormously. That is my position with relation to those two questions.
Perhaps it might be well for me to discuss for a moment the legislation of 1914, merely for the purpose of enabling us to have a clear appreciation otf the circumstances under which it was enacted.
You will remember, Sir, that at that time the owners came to Parliament and said they required 8100,(XX),000, and if we would raise 845,000,000 they would raise $58,000,-000-the proceeds of the 845,000,000 bond's we guaranteed plus the 858,000,000 being equivalent to 8100,000,000. We guaranteed the 845,000,000, and as compensation for that guarantee we obtained certain benefits, and these must always be kept in mind {Mr. R. B. Bennett.]	:
in the consideration of the problem as it now presents itself. First, we took as security for the 845,000,000 a first specific mortgage or charge upon certain properties which are set out in the schedule to the Act. But before we did that, we created the Canadian Nbrthern Railway system, which system was made up of a large number of companies, the names of which are set out in that schedule. So we have default, and there being default, there arises in the mind of this Parliament-because it is Parliament and not the Government that is charged with the responsibility-the question: What action shall we take in view of that default? The ordinary remedy for default is foreclosure. It is always open for the mortgagee to take possession, but a mortgagee's possession is always -a serious matter, and in 1914 I pointed out that I objected to the terms of the clause now under consideration, for the reason that if we exercised those powers we became mortgagees in possession, and as mortgagees in possession we'were liable for a strictness of accounting that in my judgment no Government dnd no Parliament should undertake. I made a further criticism, and it was this, that inasmuch as it is provided that in the event of default we may take possession of the physical property, there was no ready method available by which, having taken possession, we could foreclose the equity of redemption. I urged against section 24 the criticism that it could only be made effective if Parliament was in session, because it did not give to the Governor in Council any power to. foreclose the equity of redemption, but vested that power in this Parliament, and every member of this House has an equal responsibility for the exercise of that power. If authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions, if any, as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing foreclose the equity of redemption.
Let us for a moment ask ourselves what the foreclosure of the equity of redemption means. It merely means the wiping out of the stock; it merely means the destruction of it so far as value is concerned. Haying wiped out that stock, it would only be necessary to reorganize the company in the hands of the administration, and issue capital stock to the extent that might be necessary to represent the new investment the Government was putting into it. That is what is done in every reorganization plan. Some hon. gentlemen no doubt remember the reorganization plan of the Wabash last year and of the Rock Island system and of the Chicago Great Western and, more recently, within the last few weeks, the reorganization of the Missouri Pacific. What wras done in these cases was that a great financial house like Morgan's, or *Kahn, Loeb & Company make the necessary cash advance, make the necessary assessment on the old capital stock, and then reorganized with a new capitalization, sometimes with no change of name for the purpose of enabling the company to continue its corporate existence and carry on its business.
That section contemplated dealing with the determination of the compensation to be paid on the foreclosure of the equity of redemption. Of course, behind that, there is the very sound principle that this is the high court of Parliament; this is the su-

preme court of this Dominion, and it is but in keeping -with the theory of our constitution and of our institutions that when this Parliament deals with a matter, a* a high court, it has the right to determine what compensation shall be paid for the foreclosure of the equity of redemption which may belong to any person with relation to any property. This high court of Parliament, sitting as the court of last resort-the tribunal of paramount importance -has the right to determine what sum shall be paid for the foreclosure of that equity. Parliament does not necessarily act by all its members sitting together and hearing the evidence. It is not necessary that we all have to sit here and hear the witnesses, to determine what value, if any, attaches to the equity of redemption. We can designate a committee, whose report we may or may not accept, or we may determine that this high court will appoint certain referees for the purpose of taking evidence and determining what value rests upon that equity.
I cannot agree with my hon. friends opposite in saying that without hearing testimony we should decide that no value attaches to that equity of redemption. To quote the words of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, we have not yet reached that "Prussian state of affairs," but we well might say: "Is this Prussia?" if we denied to any man whose property is being taken from him the right to establish that it had some value. I put it to hon. gentlemen opposite, is it consistent with the ideas of British justice and British fair play that Mackenzie and Mann, or anybody else-and I love Them not-should be deprived of their property without having an opportunity to establish its value, if it has any? What would hon. gentlemen opposite like to have done to themselves? Is there a single gentleman who would like to have the equity of redemption of his farm for instance, taken from him without having an opportunity of being heard before the tribunal that takes it? Not long ago there was a case decided in the Supreme Court, from the province of Manitoba, in which the holding was that notwithstanding the fact that the equity of redemption had been barred and taken from a farmer years before, he was still permitted to come in, pay off his mortgage, and get back his property. It is somewhat dangerous-I emphasize the word-for a body of responsible gentlemen sitting in this Parliament at this time to say to the people of Canada 
that we deny to any person the right to establish, if he can, that there is a value to that which you take from him. There is a great feeling of unrest in this country at the present moment. Sometimes I wonder if it will find manifestation in socialism, or anarchy, or something worse. 1 entreat hon. gentlemen to pause before they say to the body of excited and disturbed public opinion in this country at this time, that you are going to take property from individuals, without affording them an opportunity to present their case before those referees who have been appointed or who will be appointed by this Parliament to determine the value attaching to the equity of redemption in the property foreclosed.
There is another feature I would like to mention, because it appears to me to be rather important. I wonder if any honourable gentlemen have thought, as I am sure many of you have in days gone by, upon what rests that right of every man to have presented before any tribunal to which he may be directed the value of property that may be taken from him. Let us see what the Magna Charta said ^about it. It is a long time ago since John met the barons at Runnymede. By article 38, of the famous document, it was enacted and declared that no man should be dispossessed of his property except by due process of law. Upon this has been laid the foundation of the Constitution of the United States, and upon this it has always been open to the poorest citizen of this realm to go to any properly constituted tribunal and ask that his rights he respected.

Unless this Bill is amended in essential provisions, in my judgment it does injustice to the Canadian people, and a most serious and violent injustice, and works a wrong the extent of which cannot be measured in dollars. Let me present the case. What is the principle of the Bill now before the House? First of all it provides for the acquisition of shares in the Canadian Northern railway. That principle is sound. The Bill, however, says that His Majesty in Council is to enter into an agreement, and that agreement is between the owners and the pledgees of not less than five-sixths of the capital stock, for a price to be determined by arbitration. Since when were pledges introduced into this Parliament? If the hon. minister makes an agreement, he can only make it with the men who own the shares, and as the owners of the shares have pledged them he is going to make the pledgees a party to this agreement, instead of utilizing the power given him under the statute to which I have just directed attention.
Why should a third party be introduced in, this transaction? Why should any pledgee, however eminent, be introduced into this transaction? What do I care who may advance money in respect to these
shares or what sum he may advance? This House was told in 1914 that Mackenzie, Mann & Company and Mackenzie and Mann controlled these shares or owned them, and any man who took a pledge of them took it in knowledge of the statute and of that fact, and therefore it follows that this House should exercise the power given to it to take these shares and this property without regard to the rights of pledgees whose rights have arisen only since that statute, if the facts were as stated in 1914.
Let me go further. Are these pledgees to have anything to say in fixing the value before the referees? Let me put this illustration. Suppose that in 1915 I had gone to the bank to borrow $100,000, and suppose that I had put up as collateral 800 shares of Winnipeg Street railway. That stock was then worth $209 a share; to-day it is worth $36. Suppose I supplemented my collateral in 1915 by putting up some Canadian Northern stock. Obviously, since the Street Railway shares have fallen to a lesser sum than the amount of the loan, suppose some value now attaches to the Canadian Northern Railway collateral, are the pledgees to fix the value of the shares by indicating the sum advanced upon them? I submit that the very moment that we untertake to acquire these shares by agreement with pledgees that very moment we undertook to deal with a third party with whom we should -not deal. Nothing would drive me from that position. You may argue that these men are like second mortgagees, and have a right to be heard before the referee. The only right they have is the right to be paid off, so far as that is concerned. The position is clear. The only right they have is the right to register, and if they do not register, the only person to deal with is the registered owner, and no one else. That is so elementary, that no bank taking collateral ever hesitates to place upon the register the name of its manager or of the bank itself as the owner of the shares held as collateral. The people's money should not be left in the hands of any Government, to be dealt with as they may see fit, without regard to Parliament. Parliament is responsible, and not the Government. Section 3 of the Bill reads as follows:
3. (1) So soon as the said five-sixths ot the said shares have been transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may assist the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or any company included in the Canadian Northern Railway System, in paying and settling any indebtedness of such company or postponing the payment thereof on such terms as may be agreed upon, and for such purposes may make advances out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, may guarantee payment in whole or in part, and may give the obligations or securities of the Government in connection therewith.
As a matter of principle, we should have added to the* section the following words:
"For the year 1917-1918 not exceeding 

dollars." I make this suggestion because it is in accordance with constitutional precedent. It is not a sound doctrine that Parliament should give a blank cheque to any man, no matter how eminent he may be, with respect to domestic enterprises of a character such as this. In war time conditions differ, and it may be necessary to depart from ordinary rifles, for war purposes. But the power and supervision of this Parliament must be always exercised. If Parliament is true to its traditions, and to the functions for which it is created, it should see that money is voted for a specific purpose, and that we should limit the extent to which aid must be given. That is a small point, but it is essential to consider it, as part of the principle of the Bill.
Then we come to the next principle, that of arbitration, and with regard to that question I should like to make rather extended remarks. Personally, I believe it would be better to submit this matter to arbitration than to a single judge, for a reason which I will mention to this House. A -judge, under his oath of office, dealing with evidence strictly as evidence, and hearing testimony, would probably arrive at conclusions, having regard to the conditions of the law with respect to compensation (to which I shall presently refer), that might bring about results which, in my judgment, would involve very far-reaching consequences. The proposition is to appoint a tribunal ccmposed of three men, one to be
selected by Parliament, because Parliament must give its approval in general terms. The Government admits that. The railway is to appoint another member of the tribunal, and then an umpire is to be selected. That enables those arbitrators, in the very terms of the reference, to consider the whole situation, not only from' the standpoint of evidence, but from their own judgment with relation to it. My hon. friend from Pictou raised a question which seemed to me to be of some importance, because he said:
" How can these arbitrators arrive at conclusions based upon their own judgment?"
I remembered, then, a case in which I had been interested that came from Edmonton, McKinnon vs. the Calgary and Edmonton railway. That case was carried to the Supreme Court of Canada, and is reported in 43 Supreme Court Reports, page 379. I will read a short summary of the judgments.
In expropriation proceedings under the Railway Act, the arbitrators in making their award stated that they had not found the expert evidence a valuable factor in assisting them in their conclusions, and that, after viewing the property in question they had reached their conclusion-	-
These were their words:
"Reasoning from their own judgment, and a few actual facts in evidence."
Hon. gentlemen will observe that this Bill uses the words " their own judgment ". Those are the exact words the Supreme Court of Canada had to deal with. In the first instance, the Supreme 'Court of Alberta set aside the award, and increased the compensation, but the Supreme Court of Canada held that the award should be sustained, as it was not apparent from the language that the arbitrators proceeded without proper consideration of the evidence adduced, or upon what was not properly evidence. Therefore, they sustained the award. I, therefore, take it that the creation of such a tribunal of referees as I have stated would better safeguard the interests of the Canadian people, because there are few .men that could be selected i n Canada that, in the exercise of their own judgment, have not some knowledge of the operations of the gentlemen wbo own this system. I say that, under those circumstances, the selection of a tribunal to arbitrate value, rather than submission to a court, will bring about a result that, in my judgment, will be better in keeping with the desire of the Canadian people.
But let us go a step further. There is provision for an appeal, and the appeal is subject to there being a difference of opin-

lion among the arbitrators. Well, why appoint an umpire, if you are going to appeal in case of disagreement? Usually, the right cf appeal is not dependent upon there being a lack of unanimity, but in this case the right of appeal has been said to he subject to there being a lack of unanimity on the part of the referees or arbitrators. I am not disposed to question that. It seems to me that i3 a very excellent provision, but if you are going to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada upon a question of law and fact, it is also proper that the interests of this country should be very well safeguarded with respect to those three words "their own judgment." To that extent, exceeding care must be exercised before the tribunal with reference to that phase of it. If an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada is granted, in my judgment there should be the right of the Crown- which I believe was the subject of a paragraph in an international arbitration on one occasion-that if the amount of the award is, in the opinion of the Crown, too large, it may repudiate the award. Some such safeguard might well be thrown about this matter, in order to fix a maximum, to give to the Crown the right, in the event of there being a difference of opinion, of declining to take up the award. It is always open to a party to say whether or not he shall take up an award; people refuse very frequently to take up awards and pay the costs. There is no reason why such a provision should not be inserted in this Bill.
These are minor matters, but I submit there is one matter which is the crux of this whole section, with relation to arbitration. What is to be arbitrated? If the House will be good enough to observe the words of the section, they are as follows:
The said arbitrators shall determine the value of the 600,000 shares.
That raises a question of paramount importance. How is "value" ito be determined? I listened to the remarks of my hon. friends opposite, and I listened to the arguments of the hon. members on this side of the House, but I received little or no light with reference to it. I read the statement of Professor Swain, in the findings of the Drayton-Acworth Commission, but with little assistance. Now, what is to be determined is the value of the shares. Let us ask ourselves first of all, what legal principles guide and determine value? The first valuation of a railway line on the American continent was in the state of

The state of Wisconsin then took up the question and, as this House knows, the Congress of the United States provided for the creation of a tribunal to determine the physical value of the railways of the U ited States, and they fixed how that work should be done. The State of Kansas provided how the work should be done with relation to the railways in that state, and I am going to direct the attention of this House, for a moment, to the particular observation quoted from the report of Professor Swain, by the hon. Minister of Finance. The other day that hon. minister referred to Professor Swain's report, and pointed out the difficulties that eminent gentleman mentioned in determining what constituted value. Value is one of the most difficult things in the world to determine with relation to a railway, and if this Bill goes through this House as it now stands, there is no reason, indeed, why the expectations of my hon. friend from Pictou should not be realized, and that the owners of the Canadian Northern should not get $100,000,000. Let us turn to what Professor Swain said with respect to value. On page 5 of his report, he says:
To determine this physical value there are two, and only two, available bases:-
(1)	The original cost, or original cost less depreciation, according to circumstances;
(2)	The cost of reproducing the property at or about the time the valuation is made, or, the cost of reproduction new less depreciation, according to circumstances.
There are the two methods: Which one of them is to be adapted in this case? Wil' the basis of the valuation be the reprodac tive cost now less depreciation, or will it be the initial cast? The authorities in England and in the United States, and the authorities who have written on the subject are conclusive that what Professor Swain says on this point is absolutely correct in law. There are only two bases upon which the value should be determined: the original cost less depreciation, according to the circumstances, and the cost of reproducing the property at or about the time the valuation is made. If the eminent counsel representing the owners .and pledgees of the stock appear before that tribunal, they will contend that valuation should be made upon the basis of the reproductive cost of

the road to-day, less depreciation. Does this House, does the minister, for one single moment realize what that would mean? I protest most vigorously against leaving the words of the clauses as they are, and open to such a construction. It cannot be denied that Professor Swain speaks with authority. These gentlemen, therefore, representing the owners and pledgees of the stock would come before the tribunal and pile up, day after day, evidence respecting the present reproductive cost of the property, showing the cost of structures, grades, fencing, bridges, cars and power. I appeal to the Minister of Finance to prevent this wrong being done to the Canadian people, to prevent the cost now less the depreciation being taken, for the Canadian Northern Railway company is, as we all know, owing to its limited resources, under an enormous deferred maintenance charge, and is not kept up to the same standard of efficiency as is to be found on the Canadian Pacific to-day. There are three things these men have done to this country. First, they have exploited the credit of the provinces to their detriment and, in some cases, to their ruin. ' Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Solicitor General): Mr. Speaker, some three years ago I had to do intimately with legislation which concerned the subject now before the House. That legislation has had the effect of making the problem with which we are

I agree that it should not, but I say that it will.

I am willing to trust to the arbitrators, and particularly to the Government arbitrator, the Chief Justice of Ontario. Why, there are companies in Canada to-day, as there have always been, and as there are in every country, who have a surplus of assets over liabilities in huge amounts, but who, by virtue of conditions which confront them, cannot pay a dividend on their stock, and could not sell their stock for anything at all. If there is one principle which is common to all arbitrations, if there is one principle that, better than another, expresses what is before an arbitration board or an expropriation tribunal, it is that the value of what is to be condemned is the value of that property in a fair and normal market. Consequently the proper way to approach this thing is for us to establish a tribunal which will stake the value, not of the physical assets and deduct from that the liabilities, as would be the case in expropriation, but to take the stock itself and to decide what, in a fair and normal market, all things considered the potential earning power, the present earning power, the assets behind the road, the liabilities behind the road,' all things considered, would be fair and reasonable for this country to pay. That is the course we are pursuing at the present time.

Now, we have to determine what these terms and conditions shall be.
It is true we have power to confiscate, but I ask, what principle should govern this Government? I answer that the principles that should govern us in disposing of the equity of redemption are the clear principles of equity and honour, and not the principle of confiscation.
It has been argued that, by the legislation of 1914, as interpreted on behalf of the Government in this House, automatically, upon default, the equity of redemption vanished by Order in Council. Where is such a provision to be found in that legislation, and who said it on the floor of the House? Certainly I never said it. I invite hon.

gentlemen, and particularly the hon. member from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), to point to any sentence I uttered on that occasion which, by any possibility, could be so interpreted.
We took no such power. We made no contract to automatically extinguish the equity of redemption. Is that done in ordinary life? When payment on a mortgage is in default, is the mortgagee given power to say that the equity of redemption is 'at an end, and that he can extinguish it or appropriate it to himself? Is that Common Law? No, the mortgagee is compelled, by the courts and legislation of our country, to determine the value of the equity of redemption, and to see that the mortgagor gets that value. How is the value determined? It is determined by compelling the mortgagee to put the equity of redemption up for public auction, and the highest bidder becomes the owner of the equity of redemption. In ordinary life that is determined in a fair and reasonable way, by so disposing of the equity of redemption. Is that method available to us to-day? Should we (have applied the method ordinarily applied in disposing of real and personal property? Will anybody 'suggest that we should have done it? It might have been done, and if it were what would be the result? Who in all probability would have been the highest bidder for this stock, which represents the equity of redemption of this company, if the Government had put it up for sale at public auction in the open markets of the world, even under conditions such as the present? I do not hear any answer, but I know what is in the back of the head of the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). The answer would be: the 'Canadian Pacific Railway. And why? Because the Canadian Pacific has more to gain by the purchase of that stock and the stock would have been worth more to them than to any other individual or company upon earth. The fair and inevitable presumption is that a resort to the method suggested would have landed that stock in the possession of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Could thiis Government ever have pursued that course? Would that have been in the interest of Canada? Do hon. gentlemen opposite think that should have been done? We had the power to dispose of that stock and equity of redemption as we liked by the legislation of 1914. That course was closed to us by the ordinary principles of national prudence, because this country
would not now be a party to the amalgamation of the Canadian Northern with the Canadian Pacific. of no value and we will appropriate it. That is confiscation, and that is the policy-and I hope the last policy-of hon. gentlemen opposite. Who ever heard of resorting to the report of an ex parte commission to determine the value of property in this or any other land? The terms of the agreement which will follow this measure will be entirely within the jurisdiction of and may be dictated by the Government; the shareholders, if they do not adhere to the terms stipulated in the agreement, will have to submit to the other alternative. Under the agreement the Government and the people of Canada will become, in effect, the owners of some 9,500 miles of railway and of about twenty-nine different companies operating various national utilities in every part of Canada. In proportion to our population, we become I think, the owners and operators of the largest system in any country in the world. We are .entering upon a tremendous undertaking, an undertaking that will demand the energy, the co-operation and the strength of the Canadian people; an undertaking that will be difficult, but which, if it fairly succeeds, will redound to the honour of this country. I know that there are objections to government ownership and to government operation. I believe that those objections are largely removed by retaining the corporate entity instead of providing for direct government ownership and operation. That is a fundamental requirement of the Drayton-Acworth report and of the Smith report; and that is why in the main, we adopt this method of disposing of the equity of redemption. If we followed specifically the Act of 1914, the Canadian Northern Railway Company would still continue to exist but it would not own the Canadian Northern Railway; that would be owned directly by the Government of Canada and would require to be operated by the Government or be subjected to the control of a new company created for the purpose. The method we follow under this Bill is in principle and in substantial effect the method devised and outlined by section 24 of the legislation of 1914. If we followed it literally rather than in this parallel way, we would for all practical purposes abolish the company; we would become directly the owners of the road. Furthermore, if in disposing of the equity in that way we had resort to arbitration, it would be the physical value that would count; we would not get the advantage that we get by bringing the matter before an arbitration board in the form of stock rather than in the form of an equity. We get an advantage by taking the stock instead of taking the physical road. Therefore, while in principle and in effect we follow precisely the line of section 24 of the Act of 1914, we do not follow it literally. [DOT] In this way we meet
the fundamentally important and essential condition laid down by the Drayton-Acworth report and we avoid the disasters pictured this afternoon (by the member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett).
I invite the House, therefore, to the consideration of this Bill as it is, and to the adoption of the motion for the second reading. When we get into committee the subjects brought to our attention by the member for Calgary can be fully and in detail considered. In my humble judgment, we are indebted to him for directing our attention to some of the points to which he referred, which may well receive favourable consideration at the hands of the committee. In the main, however, the principle of this Bill is sound. It is better to take this step rather than to continue making advances to the road. There will be disadvantages, but rather than continue as we have been doing we had better take this step. The public, I believe, demand that we do so. The public have a right to say whether we should allow the private management to continue, or whether we should enter upon public ownership of this road. That is what the second reading of this Bill means.
The passing of this Bill will mark a tremendous advance in the domestic affairs of Canada. It will put this country in a position of advance, perhaps, of any other country in the world, outside of Germany, in respect of government ownership of utilities. It will enable us to show, once and for all, whether government ownership of a tremendous enterprise like this is or is not a sound principle

Mr. Speaker, my views on the principle of the Bill before the House aTe so well known that probably little would be gained by my taking up the time of the House this afternoon in enlarging upon them. As I realize that it is desired that a vote should be taken before six o'clock, I shall occupy the attention of the House for only a few minutes.
In 1914 I directed some attention to the subject now under discussion, as to whether or not it was advisable that Canada should take a first step in the acquisition of her railroads, or whether it was advisable that we Should go on as we have been doing for many years, that is, subsidizing the railroads in this country. At the time I spoke in 1914, I had given some consideration and research to the problem of public ownership of railways in Canada,

and I was not unaware of ithe divergence of viewis there had been in the .past as to whether or not government ownership was a wise thing in this country. I quite appreciate the fact that, in the early days, Papineau, the great French leader, was opposed to public ownership. I realize also what a struggle there was in the 50's .and 60's in Canada as to whether the Government should themselves construct or whether they should permit private capital to construct those great new highways of steam that were coming into existence. Any one who has read the history of Nova Scotia cannoit be blind to the fact that Joseph Howe, that brilliant statesman, put up a magnificent fight that the railroads should belong to the people; that they should control those highways, and he felt that otherwise, in the days to come, they would be a source of corruption and irregularities in the public life of Canada. Sir Francis Hincks, the Inspector General of Upper Canada, seems to have held very divergent views on the subject. In the early days he was in favour of public ownership of railroads, but after coming into contact with .a great contracting firm in England, he seems to have changed his views, and when the project of the Grand Trunk railway wias launched in Upper Canada he leaned to the view that it should be constructed by private enterprise rather than by the Government. It is, however, of very little avail to discuss to-day the question as to which of those men were right or wrong. When one compares the history of the 60's with that of 1917, one must be impressed by the fact thiat the men of the former generation had exactly the same problems to face that confront u-s here to-day. Subsequently to the construction of the Grand Trunk railway, Canada was confronted with the problem whether she should take over the railroad or whether she should give aid. She guaranteed bonds; she gave subsidies; she assisted in every way possible the needs of the railway, but the lessons of those days seem to have been forgotten in the later period of our history, and we havte plunged into an orgy of giving cash subsidies and guaranteeing bonds that has brought us for solution the problem which the men of the sixties had to face.
To give the House some idea of the progress Government ownership and operation of railroads Las made, I might direct the attention of the House to the fact that in 1880 there were in the world only 10,000

miles of railways under Government operation and ownership, whereas at the present time there are 225,000 miles of railways under Government operation and ownership. Sweden, Germany, Italy-practically all-in all 55-the great countries of the world now own or operate their railways. I would be wrong if I were to say that they all do, because I would leave out the two great countries of the world that have not yet adopted a policy of government ownership. I refer to Great Britain and the United States, and yet the trend in that direction is so strong that it was but a year ago, when I was at a lunch given, by Sir John 'Hadfield'e firm to certain visiting parliamentary delegates in England, that I heard Sir John Hadfield say that, if England were to maintain her position in the industrial world after the termination of this war, it was absolutely necessary that she should control and operate her railroads. The war has demonstrated that this is practical and possible, because when the war broke out and England realized that she must control [DOT] her transportation, she took over and put under the control of the managers of the railways, representative business men and representatives of the War Office, the entire railway undertaking of Great Britain, and I do not believe any man will deny that that course has worked satisfactorily and well. The United States still maintains a system of private ownership and operation. That system is well entrenched there, and the railway interests have a great hold on the legislative bodies of the United States. I cannot say how soon that hold will be loosened. My good friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) this afternoon drew the attention of the House to the fact that many of the American railroads had gone through the hands of the receivers, and that would seem to indicate that private ownership in the United States has not been the success that might be desired for it. We in Canada, in taking over this railway, are taking a great step forward, and if I understand aright the purport of the Bill, there are two great principles in it. The first is that Canada should assume the ownership of this rail-wtay, and indirectly, through a board of directors, operate it, the object being to have the advantage of public ownership without the disadvantages, to free the railroad as far as possible from political influence or interference. The other great underlying principle of the Bill is that, if the stock has any value, the men who own the stock should be paid for their property.

As to the first principle, I think I have made it abundantly clear that I approve it, and as to the second principle, I wish to take the same position as I took in this House an 1914, and that is, if Mackenzie and Mann-I do not think there is any gentleman here who is carried away with the belief that I have any serious love for them-can prove that this stock has any value, they should be paid for it. That is my position here this afternoon.
I am opposed to the amendment as offered by the Opposition, because I think it enunciates the principle that, because a tribunal, on ex parte evidence that did not represent the views of all interested, reached the conclusion that a man's property was worth nothing, the State, by the inherent power that it has, should deprive that man of his property, without a hearing and an opportunity to prove its value. That is not sound, and it is not a wise doctrine to promulgate in this country. Whether this matter should be referred to the Exchequer Court or whether the value of this road should 'be determined by arbitration is a question on which much might be said on either side. That is a matter of detail. But if a tribunal is properly constituted-'and that is indicated by the fact that Sir William Meredith is to represent the Government on it-the matter will be fairly investigated and a fair price reached for the stock of the Canadian Northern railway.

In my judgment, it makes no difference in the world as to the value of a stock whether, if it is handed over to me as collateral security, I advance 75 per cent on it, or whether I advance 10 per cent. If the stock is to be taken over by arbitration, the inherent value of the stock, not the amount of money I advanced on it, is the determining factor, and if I understand aright the principle of the Bill, that is what the Minister of Finance understands by the second paragraph of section 4. In fairness to the pledgees, he further says: if you wish to appear before the tribunal and be heard, that is your privilege. You have advanced money on this security and you have certain rights. I am not so confident, however, as to whether or not the hon. member for Calgary is not right in his second position, namely, that the cost of reconstruction is not something that might well be directed to the attention of the arbitrators in determining the value. You will observe, Sir, that subsection 2 of paragraph 4 says:
The said arbitrators shall determine thle value of the said six hundred thousand shares as of the date of the said agreement, and the said arbitrators shall proceed in a summary way and may apply their own judgment in determining such value, and may receive witn respect thereto such reports and statements authenticated in such way as they may decide and such evidence as they may deem necessary or helpful, examine witnesses under oath and hear parties by counsel or representatives, and the unanimous determination of the arbitrators shall be final.
It seems to me it might be advocated before the arbitrators on the part of the company that this stock has a potential value, that it has ajpotential earning power; and that, as the great bulk of the money that had gone into the undertaking had gone into it when the materials were less valuable than they are to-day, in determining the value of the stock, the present value of the physical assets as such should be considered as well as the potentialities of the road. It seems to me, therefore, that that is a matter that might have the attention of the Solicitor General and the Minister of Finance, so that when the measure comes before the House in committee they might be in a position to advise us as to what the best legal advisors of the Government think in reference to this contention.
The five minutes that I promised to take have more than run, but I would again like to aver that my vote shall be cast in favour of the Bill, because I think it declares for a very long step in the advancement of Canada's policy in reference to her railway construction, maintenance and operation.

Mr, GRAHAM: Before His Majesty acquires these shares of capital stock, I think we ought to have some assurance from the Government that contractors who have just claims against Mackenzie and Mann, either as contractors or as owners of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway should be paid. Mackenzie, Mann & Company as contractors construct the road for Mackenzie and Mann as owners. There are various subsidiary companies making up the Canadian Northern Railway system. In the different provinces the road, main line and branches, has been constructed under charters with different names. In Ontario it is called the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway, in Quebec the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway. In British Columbia the road was constructed under a provincial charter, called the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway. These several companies make up the Canadian Northern Railway system. Mackenzie, Mann & Company as contractors constructed most of these lines for Mackenzie and Mann as owners of the railway. My contention is that the Government, in taking over all this property, takes the place of Mackenzie, Mann & Company, contractors, or Mackenzie and Mann, owners of the road, and should become responsible for all their just liabilities. I pointed out on the second reading that, of necessity, the Government will have to assume these liabilities. Several contractors who have performed work in this connection claim that they have not received their pay and have not been able to make any progress during the last two or three years towards getting their money. I know the Government could say in taking over the Canadian Northern Railway system that technically it is not responsible for the liabilities of Mackenzie and Mann as contractors or of any of their sub-contractors. But this is the situation: If the Government is -taking over, under a statute, property which has not been paid for, it certainly should pay for that property; buying the capital stock from the holders of the capital stock does not at all relieve the Government but rather involves the Government in the payment of these accounts. I do not pretend to say that every hatched-up account or every account that can be hatched up should be paid by the Government, but
I do say that where a contractor proves a legitimate claim this Government cannot in equity refuse to pay that contractor for work done on the highway that the government is taking over under statute. If these same men had built a house, as mechanics, they would have taken liens on the house, and no matter who purchased the house the liens would be enforceable. So I say, that although as railway contractors they cannot take liens on this property; in equity the Government ought to pay to these contractors every just claim.

Up to the time my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) spoke this afternoon, the Government, as I recall their attitude since this discussion opened, did not manifest any disposition to accept suggestions by way of improvement of the method or the details of carrying out the transaction to which the Bill now before the committee relates. However, after the hon. gentleman from Calgary had spoken, and had delivered what I think, in the opinion of this House, was one of the most incisive, complete and masterly analyses of any measure ever submitted to Parliament, the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), who followed him, realized the position in which the Government and its Bill had been placed by that speech. The Solicitor General proceeded to indicate that in regard to certain matters of principle, and in re-gard-to other matters of detail, the suggestions made by the member for Calgary would probably receive consideration. The Minister of Finance will recall that a complaint, voiced, perhaps, with more effectiveness by the member for Calgary than by any other speaker in this discussion-although he was not by any means the only one who voiced it-was made as to the incompleteness of the information laid before the House with regard to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has dealt with one branch of that aspect of the discussion. He has pointed out that there are a number of unsettled contractors' claims. He has argued that these contractors, having built the road which is to be taken over by the Government, having put up some of their own money in connection with that work, should be paid for their services and that the Government should assume responsibility for the debts so owed these contractors. I have knowledge of some of those claims. I recall some claims that were submitted to me by contractors who did work on the Sudbury-Port Arthur line, a branch of the Canadian Northern system which was constructed by the Mackenzie and Mann company. So far as I know, these claims have not yet been settled. One claim at least in connection with the construction of the telegraph line along that system has not yet been settled; there may be others. I could give the details and verify these before the Bill goes out of committee. But if the minister will admit the principle that the Government should pay these men, who have given value to the company, then we could postpone the discussion of the details.
Another very important matter was touched upon by the member for Calgary, to which allusion had not previously been made, and which the hon. Solicitor General found it convenient to overlook in what he described as his reply. I refer to the member for Calgary's enumeration of the existing liabilities in connection with unfinished

contracts for which the Government will become liable under the terms of their proposed legislation. Let me direct the attention of the minister and of the" committee to the situation in that regard as it exists in British Columbia in connection with the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway. A news item in the Vancouver Sun of August 11, 1917, is as follows:
Viotoria, Aug:. 10.-The following telegram sent by Hon. John Oliver, minister of rhjil -ways, to Sir R. L. Borden to-day:
"British Columbia has guaranteed the principal and interest on forty-seven million nine hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars of Canadian Northern Pacific railway company bonds and has contracts obligating the railway company to expend twenty-two to twenty-five millions to complete. Are the province's interests being protected? Please reply quickly.
The under-mentioned reply from Sir R. L. Borden has been received :
"The Government proposes to acquire all the capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway company which owns all the stock of the Canadian Northern Pacific railway company. Copy of the bill now before Parliament is forwarded to-day for your consideration. The company's obligations will remain as they were before such acquirement."
The newspaper item proceeds:
By Sir Robert Borden's telegram it will be seen that the Dominion Government assumes all the Canadian Northern railway's obligations in respect to the Canadian Northern Pacific railway, both financial and as to the completion by the latter railway of its existing contracts.
If the statement of the Premier of British Columbia be correct, there is an obligation of between $22,000,000 and $25,000,000. I submit that this committee is entitled to full information, not only in regard to this particular outstanding obligation, but also in regard to all other obligations coming within that category. That is information which, I think, should have been regarded as included in the general request for information made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. That is the second point upon which I should like the hon. minister to furnish the committee with details before we proceed to a consideration of the Bill.
I wish to refer to another matter in connection with which the committee is entitled to the fullest information. We have had discussion as to the pledgees of the stock, the holders of bonds and other individuals or interests who will be affected by or who are bound to become beneficiaries under this legislation. Information was asked from the minister as to the identity of these individuals and interests, but so far as I am aware that information has not yet been given to the committee. I

wish to recall the incident through which the Minister of Finance was brought into public life. I refer to the letter that was signed by the eighteen gentlemen in Toronto in the spring of 1911 against reciprocity. The minister Was one of those eighteen gentlemen. The complete list of the eighteen is given in the Canadian Annual Review for 1911.	_
So-called Liberals?

'I would ask the minister to state to the committee whether, excluding himself, the gentlemen named, or the executors or the representatives of -the estates of those who have died, hold any of this stock, or are the pledgees of this stock, or are the

holders of any of those Canadian Northern bonds, and whether Sir Clifford Sifton is the owner or holder of stock or the pledgee of any of those bonds. The committee should have that information in order properly to appreciate the legislation before tire House. I, therefore, invite my hon. friend to give to the committee the information under the three heads I have enumerated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
has considerable imagination to link up a letter signed by eighteen Liberals in Toronto against reciprocity with the question now before the committee. My hon. friend has read the names of eighteen very distinguished citizens of Toronto. He will admit that the names are all good, and that they were quite within their rights in signing the letter they did in regard to the issue of reciprocity, just as hon. gentlemen opposite have been quite within their rights in voting against their leader on the question of compulsory military service. My hon. friend asks me if I know whether any of those gentlemen whose names he has mentioned are in any way interested in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway company. As a matter of knowledge, I do not know any shareholder or* bondholder to-day of the Canadian Northern Railway company, and the only information I have is this, that I believe that Mackenzie, Mann & company, Limited, are the owners of 51 per cent of the stock cf the Canadian Northern Railway company. It would he a matter of surprise to me if the gentlemen mentioned, Sir John Eaton, Mr. Allan, Mr. George, Mr.
Mr. Lash.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Last! is second vice-president of the Canadian Northern ; Mr. Woods is vice-president or director of fhe Canadian Northern; as to the others, so far as I am aware they are not in any way connected with the Canadian Northern as stockholders or bondholders. I should1 be surprised to learn that he had any personal interest in the enterprise. I do not know .any of the bondholders of the Canadian Northern, and, as I say, the only stockholders of whom I am aware are first, the Minister of Finance and Receiver General who owns $40,000,000 worth of stock, and, secondly, Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann & company, Limited, who are the owners
of about 51 per cent, that is, they have a controlling interest in the Canadian Northern Railway company.
