speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Lash is second vice-president of the Canadian Northern. Whether Mr. Lash holds any shares, and if so to what extent he is a shareholder, I am not aware. The bondholders are largely in Great Britain. The Canadian Northern has always been known as a close corporation, the principal stock being held by Mackenzie, Mann & Company, Limited. I have no further information with regard to the others, and I should be much surprised to learn that any considerable number of them, if any of them other than those who are officially connected with fhe company, are bondholders or stockholders in the Canadian Northern Railway company.

Will the minister get
that information? I can quite understand he might not have it himself, but the information ought to be obtained and placed before the committee. We ought also to know, in the same connection the indebtedness of fhe Canadian Northern Railway company to the Canadian Bank of Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not the
information as to the indebtedness of the Canadian Northern to the Canadian Bank of Commerce nor to any other bank. The statements laid upon the Table show the floating indebtedness of the Canadian Northern -railway.
With regard to the claims mentioned by tiie lion, member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), the position is this: The Dominion Government is acquiring the shares of the Canadian Northern Railway Company; that is to say, instead of the present shareholders, the Dominion Government will be the sole shareholders. The corporate organizations of the company as well as the organizations of fhe subsidiary and constituent companies will remain as at present, the intention being to administer them as corporations, that is to say as they are being administered at present. The claims against those companies can he filed with the Department of Railways precisely as they are being filed to-day. The financial controller of railways, who is here to-night, tells me there aTe comparatively few claims against Mackenzie, Mann & company,



Limited, in connection with, the Montreal to Pert Arthur section. I ha vie the details of them here. There are five altogether, and there is in the department $72,000, or nearly enough to cover those claims, the amount involved being approximately $80,000. The department lakes up those claims and looks into them carefully. The ca6e referred to by the hon. member for South Renfrew has been under the most careful consideration of the Kailway Department.
It has been outstanding tor four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The claim is contested, and, in the opinion of the Railway Department, justly contested. The Department of Railways offered a mode of settling the question by having a re-measurement. The contractors agreed to that.
When was that offer made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Three or four
weeks ago, and I understand the mode of determination suggested has not been adopted by the gentlemen in question. The Dominion Government could not undertake to pay claims which are usually filed for the largest possible amount. The Dominion Government takes over the Canadian Northern Railway company, and that company continues just as it has in the past. Any claims which in the past could have been filed can now be filed. The Department of Railways, as my hon. friend knows, retains moneys from subsidies and from the proceeds of guaranteed securities for the purpose of covering those claims.
If the claim of which I have spoken is found to be a just claim, will it be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the Department of Railways says so. The money is in the Department of Railways for that purpose.

The difficulty has been this: the claim has been outstanding for years, and the contractors could never get the company to say whether the claim was a just one or not. The company would not go into particulars, but stood the contractor off, by saying they would send the engineer to look over the work. They never did so, however, except that a man once went over it in a motor truck, which goes at 25 miles an hour, and he could not see anything. I know something about this claim, because I attempted to get it settled, not months but years ago. The engineer did not make

any examination at all of the work, I am informed, and the company have always refused to get down to close quarters in considering it. I would not ask the Government to pay a claim that was not just for this contractor or anybody else, but now that the Government has taken over the road I should like to be assured that if this is a just claim the Government will see that it is paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There will be no different procedure from that of the past, because the Department of Railways will still be the Department of Railways and will still investigate these claims. The Department of Railways, which is a department of the Dominion Government, has the money to pay these claims, provided they are just. 'My hon. friend does not suggest that the department should pay unjust claims?
No, I made that clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point I make with regard to the stock we are purchasing is that it does not affect these claims at all. As the department has the money to pay the claims, no question arises as to funds, and, therefore, it is only a question of the contractors or the sub-contractors establishing their claim to the satisfaction of the department. With all due respect to my hon. friend, I do not see that we should hold up the consideration of this Bill on any such consideration as he has put forward, because, as I have said, the money is in the department to pay the claims if they are just.
WTdll the minister tell us just what he means by saying that the Department of Railways have the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department holds a drawback. The subcontractor who has a claim against the contractor files his claim in the Department of Railways, which has moneys belonging to the company.
Subsidy money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, or proceeds of guaranteed bonds which it holds back. So the fact of the Government becoming the owner of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company does not alter the situation in the least degree. The subcontractor with a just claim can still file his claim with the Department of Railways against the railway. The claims that have been mentioned are under investigation by the department, and there is no doubt that it has the money to pay the claims if they

are established. The financial comptroller of the Department of Railways informs me that in the first case drawn to onr attention by the hon. member for South Renfrew, a reasonable proposal has been made to the subcontractor, but it has not been accepted, I believe. .
I know what it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend asked me with reference to the bondholders and stockholders of the Canadian Northern Railway company. I have no information whatever, nor do I believe it could be obtained, with regard to the bonds, because they pass from hand to hand. With regard to the stock, I understand that Mackenzie, Mann & Company, Limited, are the owners of about 51 per cent of the stock, which is sufficient to make operative the agreement referred to in section 1 of the Bill. As to who the other stockholders are, representing one-sixth of the capital stock, I have no information. Some are in England. I understand that the Government of British Columbia is also a shareholder. But Mackenzie, Mann & Company, being the owners of 51 per cent of the stock, are in the position to lodge stock and make operative the agreement under section 1. Then it is open to others to bring in their shares, and if they do not bring lin their shares the Governor in Council may declare that those remaining shares are vested in His Majesty subject to the terms of this legislation.

I know the modus oper-andi of the Railway Department pretty well and 1 know that in the case I have referred to the chief contractor can put obstacles in the way of the adjustment of the claim and postpone settlement year after year. He may say, for instance, that the road is in a state of semi-completion. That happened with me time and again. I .have often had to call in tihe chief contractor and say: " If you won't say something about this claim one w.ay or the other, I am going to pay this subcontractor." I have done that on several occasions. Now that the Government is becoming owner of the road, it is in a position to act in unison with the Railway Department and' act more promptly than the former owners of the stock. What I am trying to draw from the Government is a statement that they will take these claims up and have them adjusted, and not act as the former railway company did, which postponed the claims year after year. All I ask is that if a just claim is established it will be paid. I understand

that there are only some $72,000 worth of claims to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Some of these
claims are too high.

Some may have to be reduced. The point I am making is that when the Government takes over the road it ought to see that these men who have done work for the company shall be settled with, and should it happen that the arbitrators find that the common stock has.a value the Government would be in. a position absolutely to recoup itself for any expenditures it might make in this way.
Sir 'THOMAS WHITE:	We have the
money anyway.
'Mr. MEJGHEN:	I have made inquiry
of the comptroller as to the specific claim mentioned by my hon. friend from South Renfrew. I believe it is the claim of Macdonald and Lynn, who were subcontractors under Mullarkey, who himself wa.s a subcontractor. It appears that the dlai n h::s been standing for some time, but the comptroller te'.ls me that it is only within very recent months that it has come before the Department of Railways and Canals.
That is true, I think.

It came before the department in this form. Macdonald and Lynn claim that the measurements were wrong. They had been paid the full apportionment coming to them, providing the measurements of the Canadian Northern railway under which Mullarkey himself took his money were correct. They claim, however, that these measurements were too small, and consequently there was more money coming to them-. The proposal made to them by the Department of Railways and Canals was that a new measurement should be made, under which Mullarkey would take a readjustment, if necessary, of his moneys, and consequently, Macdonald and Lynn a readjustment of theirs. The condition of the remeasurement was to be that if the first measurement was right Macdonald and Lynn would stand the cost of the remeasuring; if it was not right, the Canadian Northern would stand the cost. That proposal seems eminently fair, but Macdonald and Lynn have not yet acceded to it, and that is why the claim is standing. It is a matter of perfect indifference to the department, except that they would like to see the claim settled. That is the proposal that has been made, I am informed, and the ones who have not accepted it are Macdonald and Lynn.

This may 'seem a small thing, (but it is a big thing to Macdonald and Lynn, because it means practically the profit on their work. Macdonald and Lynn have begged of the Canadian Northern, or of 'Mr. Mullarkev, who is technically a subcontractor but really Mackenzie and Mann's contractor, to send a man to have these measurements taken.
They declined to send the man. Macdonald and Lynn said: "Then, we will get an engineer up and you go with him." This they also declined. Macdonald and Lynn then went to "the expense of making all the measurements themselves. The Canadian Northern declined to send a man over with them to check up the measurements. Of course, that was before it came before the Railway Department. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The controller informs me that there are some outstanding claims in respect of sub-contractors' work, and that is the reason why the drawback is held. Does it not come down to about this-there is money to pay just claims, and if a claim is established as legitimate, it will be paid? There is no question as to the money.
That is so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All my hon. friend suggests is greater activity than has existed in the past. He says that by reason of the ownership of the road being in private hands there has been delay, and that it has been under the Railway Department for investigation, and he suggests that now when the Government becomes
9 p.m. proprietor of the road there might be greater activity with a view to having this settled. But it cannot' be settled until the Railway Department determines that the claim is just. I am sure no hon. gentleman would ask the Department of Railways to pay out money in settlement of an unjust claim. I do not think we can advance the matter further than that. If the claim is legitimate, there is money to pay it, and it will be paid.

My hon. friend has become accustomed to deal in such large figures and such huge amounts of money, Aleighen.]
that he has forgotten this trifling matter of $25,000,000 in connection with the Canadian Northern Pacific.

speechtext: What $25,000,000 is that?

The $25,000,000 which the Premier of British Columbia says is necessary to complete the contracts of the Canadian Northern in that province. I asked the hon. gentleman if it was one of the obligations the Government was taking over, and how many obligations of a like character there were.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That obligation is not affected at all by what is being done here. The Canadian Northern Pacific, as my hon. friend knows, is a company whose stock is held by the Canadian Northern Railway company. After the Government acquires the capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway, the stock of the underlying company will still be held just as it is to-day, and the company will be carried on, and be responsible for such obligations as it has, just as is the case to-day. The status of the Canadian Northern Pacific, or, indeed, of any of the subsidiary or constituent companies, or of the Canadian Northern Railway company itself, is not changed. They are the same companies, with the same liabilities, and the same obligations. I am unable to pronounce offhand as to the merits of this matter. My hon. friend quotes a telegram, or a letter, from the Premier of British Columbia which is, of course, entitled to consideration.

I also quoted the reply of the Prime Minister.
, Sir THOMAS W5HITE: When the Government secures the ownership of this stock, the system will be run as it is being run to-day. The obligation will not be lost. From the standpoint of the government of British Columbia it may be a rather fortunate thing that this Government is taking over the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company. Whatever the obligations of the Canadian Northern Pacific may be, they would be more likely to be carried out with the control of the Canadian Nor. them Railway system in the strong hands of the Government than if it were in the hands of any private owners, especially in times like these. I am quite unable to give any definite answer to my hon. friend, but I may say, it does not appear to me that the point he mentions really touches what we are doing, the status of all these companies being maintained.
My hon. friend is very patient and very courteous-	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why should I not be?

-but he will pardon me if I do not enter into the discussion into which he wishes to lead me, or to lead the committee. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Department
ol Railways has only three claims on file in respect of the Canadian Northern Pacific, aggregating $170,000. Against these claims, they have $300,000 of subsidy moneys in their hands. The particular obligation to which my hon. friend refers no doubt arises out of an agreement with the Government of British Columbia. Whatever that obligation may be, it will still remain. I do not think it is possible to give definite information with regard to the extent of claims, except indebtedness, of such a system as this- a railway system extending throughout the whole of Canada, with branch lines which have beenprojected, where bonds have been sold and the proceeds deposited against construction. It would take months, or moie, to make any statement with regard to a matter of that kind. All we are doing is acquiring a great transcontinental system. There may be cases in which lines have been projected, where the company, through inability to finance, has not been able to make the extensions.
But, if they have sold the bonds on those projected extensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The proceeds
would be waiting for the construction to be made.
In all cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In all cases.

Does not the minister
think it reasonable that we should find out what this will cost? Before we embark on a transaction of this kind, w'e ought to know what the ultimate cost will toe-.

It must be clear to the hon. gentleman that a transfer of stock of any company in no way affects the obligations, whatever they may be. By this transaction the Government of Canada does not become pledged to pay any debt whatsoever. All it pays for is the stock it is getting. I did not hear the first wire read, but I understand it is in regard to some claims in respect of construction still to go on.

No. It is a telegram from the Premier of British Columbia referring to a contract 'between the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway company and the Government of British Columbia, for the construction of some line or lines, and stating that it would require from $22,000,000 to $25,000,000 to complete that contract. The Premier of British Columbia inquired if the-obligation was being taken over by the Government. '

That obligation would
not be taken over by the Government at all, and the reply of the Prime Minister would so indicate. I remember the reply, although I cannot recall its exact wording. The Government does not take over any obligation of the Canadian Northern Railway company. We take over certain stock of the company.
The obligations of the company will remain exactly the same as before. As to what the Government will do, ci rather as to what the Canadian Northern will do after it is controlled by the Government, with respect to obligations, I would say that, generally speaking, the disposition would be to carry out any honest obligations entered into in respect of construction- If there is a contract by the Canadian Northern Pacific in respect of construction, it will probably be found that there are moneys against that contract, the proceeds of securities guaranteed by the province of British Columbia; in other words, that the financing practically is already provided for by virtue of provincial legislation and contracts. Consequently while if there is a contract the obligation of the company to carry it out will be the same as before, it will not be an obligation involving net expenditure by the company because there will be moneys against it, the proceeds of guaranteed securities perhaps already realized. There is no reason for the company changing its policy in, respect to these roads.
If they had the money there would be no excuse for not going on with the contract.

Perhaps the moneys that are there are not sufficient to complete the work. Generally speaking, the company would assume the same attitude afterwards as before. It would go on with such contracts as the financial conditions permitted, and I presume the contracts read in such a manner that the option to proceed or not to proceed is open to the company; at all events, whatever was open to it before will be open to it still, and I know of no reason why the policy of the company should be changed.
What would be the policy of the Government in case contracts had been entered into to build roads that very closely duplicate other roads?

It would depend on the outlook, on the alternative courses open. I do not know of any such obligation binding on the company, and if there was an obligation for the expenditure of money that was not wise I should be very much surprised.
If the money was given them for a certain purpose it could not be used-dor another purpose?
No.

The minister has said
that what we were doing at present was taking over that stock, which is quite true. But is it not also true that we are embarking on the nationalization of a great transcontinental railway which has certain liabilities scattered over the country very generally, and that when we complete the work we are starting to do we shall own the road free from all encumbrances, and all of these things will have to be paid? I should be surprised if there were not scores of claims of which the Government has not yet heard. While we are only purchasing the stock to-day, is it not reasonable for us to ask the Solicitor General to give a statement of what he expects to pay in the end, what the ultimate liability of the country will be when we secure the road from end to end?

That is all before the House. The responsibilities of the company are shown on the balance sheet, and there is no reason to doubt its correctness. These liabilities are shown on the balance sheet as of the 30th June, 1916. Another balance sheet was taken off on the 30th April, 1917, and another is in course of preparation showing all liabilities of every kind up to the 30th June, 1917.

Will the minister give
the gross liabilities of record now?

The liabilities will be $578,000,000 less $139,000,000, about $439,000,000. I understand the total indebtedness of t'he company is under $425,000,000. That is liabilities of every kind and description. There are certain items that appear on both sides of the account, and in this way the total liabilities are reduced to less than $425,000,000.
Do Mackenzie and Mann own 51 per cent of the $60,000,000, or of the $100,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is 51 per cent of the $100,000,000. That is $51,000,000 of the $60,000,000 outstanding.
The minister has given the total amount of liabilities that Canada is assuming by this transaction.

We are no't assuming
these liabilities at all.

The company controlled by the Government will have to assume these liabilities. The Government is at the back of those liabilities and will have to make them good. Did the Minister of Finance, when this matter came to a head, convene any financiers, men of high financial ability in Canada, and tell them that the Government was committing themselves to this huge transaction, as he consulted financial experts before issuing his domestic loan? The other day when it was rumoured that the minister would issue another domestic loan, I met some of the bankers on the train from Montreal to Ottawa and I learned that they were called by my hon. friend into consultation upon that loan. I do not disapprove of that; on the contrary,
I think it is wise on the part of the Minister of Finance, before embarking upon any such large transaction, to consult, outside of Parliament, the best minds of Canada.
I should like to know whether, when he and his colleagues decided to bring this legislation before Parliament, he consulted outside of Parliament, men like the president of the Bank of Montreal, the largest institution in Canada, which in this country is something bke the Bank of England in the Old Country, or whether he consulted men of the ability of Sir Frederick Taylor and other financiers of mark in Canada, before committing the country to this transaction. I should like my hon. friend to answer the point raised by my hon. friend the ex-Secretary of State (Mr. AUGUST 16, 1917
Murphy). The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has dismissed, with a wave of the hand, the question which was put by that hon. gentleman. He asked for a list of the shareholders, bondholders and pledgees of the road, and the Minister of Finance simply answered that he did not know, and, as regards the shares of the Canadian Northern, that he understood 51 per cent were controlled by the company. We are supposed to be business men in this House. We are elected to represent the seven or eight million people who compose the population of Canada. We are committing the country to the extent of nearly half a billion dollars. We are now on the eve of making an agreement with the Canadian Northern, with a view to control the balance of the stock. I understand the hon. gentleman says that 51 per cent of that stock belongs to the Canadian Northern. It seems to me that we ought to know with whom we are going to make this bargain. If that stock is really in the hands of Mackenzie and Mann, or the Canadian Northern, or, as was reported this afternoon, partly in the hands of Sir Clifford Sifton, to the amount of $750,000, we ought to know the names of the shareholders of the Canadian Northern. My hon. friend will say, "What does it matter whether A, B or C holds a few hundred shares? You have the agreement before you. Is it a good or bad agreement?" It is important, indeed it is essential, in a transaction of that magnitude, that we should know with whom we are trading, and with whom we are trucking. There is a rumour in reference to the holding of the stock of the Canadian Northern, and my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) will forgive me if I refer to it here. I do not impugn his personal honour at all in this matter, because the hon. gentleman stated some time ago, and I accepted his word, that he had no longer any connection with the institution which has been mentioned in connection with this transaction but it is rumoured, and repeated in the press-in subdued tones, because the press is chloroformed-and in the clubs, that the men who are behind this transaction, the big shareholders of the Canadian Northern, are effectively controlling the Government. I do not say it is true, but I suspect it might be true.
The Government is going to buy out the control.
My good friend the Minister of Finance laughs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot help it.

The hon. gentleman
knows the political history of Canada for the past twenty years, surely. He was a member of the Liberal party in 1904. What happened then? Is it not a fact that the Canadian Northern in 1904 got control, a few days before nomination in the general election, of a powerful daily in Montreal, which, heretofore, had been supporting the Government; that, under the influence of the Canadian Northern, that paper made a right-about turn, just on the eve of nomination day? Is it not a fact that, at the same time, it was reported that the Canadian Northern would see that three ministers of the Crown would be arrested Sir Clifford Sitfon's name was mentioned as one of them-and that a number of candidates would be bought outright by the company, in order to get control of the Parliament to be elected in 1904? I am not repeating cock-and-bull stories. Let my hon. friend put the question to the member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). He brought the whole matter before the House in regard to the election of 1904, and hon. gentlemen will see by reference to Hansard that he stated that there had been a deliberate conspiracy by that very company to get control of the Parliament of Canada.
I am not inventing the story. It is well known, and probably my hon. friend is well aware of it. Did it succeed? The plot failed miserably.
They got a guarantee of bonds from the hon. gentleman's Government.

Let the megaphone of
Mackenzie and Mann keep silent for a few minutes. There has never been any insinuation or accusation against any of the members of the Laurier Government on account of that guarantee of bonds, and the hon. gentleman is the first to make the insinuation this evening, but it is only an insinuation worthy of him.
What is the hon. gentleman making this last half hour?

I have not been making any insinuations. I stated two things, that the people are reporting, from one end of the country to the other, that the Canadian Northern have control of this Government, and that, in this transaction, they are the powerful interests represented. I stated what is current in the city of Ottawa, that Sir Clifford Sifton is interested to the extent of $750,000 worth of shares in the Canadian Northern. That explains the

activities of some gentlemen who want to form a win-the-war party, and who want to get a union Government. Such things happen in other countries, where people are perhaps less callous than they are in Canada, 'but they do not last. In France some years ago, at the time of the Panama scandal, it was proven unfortunately that mostly all the members of the Government and of Parliament were in the hands of the Panama companies, and there was nearly a revolution in France as a result of it. In England when, a few years ago, the Marconi scandal was rumoured, it nearly destroyed the career of the present Prime Minister of England, and there was only the suspicion that he had been given a hint to speculate in Marconi shares.
It is very generally stated throughout Canada that the Canadian Northern owns and controls the present Government, and that we are now embarking on a transaction the object of which is to make richer people who are already millionaires. These people, it is said, are afraid of the future; they think that their private enterprise is not safe, and that it is better they should be made secure by public ownership. I ask the minister to be frank with the country and to state positively who are the shareholders, pledgees and bondholders who will profit by this transaction. I want to know with whom I am dealing. I do not want to act blindly; I want to deal with A, B and C. I want to know these people who will get the money out of the Canadian treasury. I am a taxpayer; I am responsible to my electors for the taxation Bills which come before this House. In that respect I will give my hon. friend my support to a certain extent, reserving my right to criticise what I believe to be unjust. I believe, however, that the Income Tax Bill proceeds upon a right principle. On behalf of my electors, who will be called upon to pay the half-billion dollars involved in this transaction, I want to know to whom this money is going. Tell me, Mr. Chairman, of any transaction-not necessarily a transaction of this importance, but any transaction-in which the parties are not known by their names?
The North Atlantic Trading Company.

My hon. friend, in order to make some defence of the scandalous proposal that we are now considering, is obliged to refer to the North Atlantic Trading Company. Did he approve of the absence of names in that case?
I was not here.
Why does tny hon. friend mention it, then?
Because the hon. gentleman approved it.
Yes, I approved it; but if I was wrong, is the hon. gentleman right to-day?
We are not doing the same|thing.
If at that time the Government was misled by its agent in England, is my hon. friend right to-day?
Certainly we are right.

My hon. friend is ready to involve the credit of this country to the extent of $439,000,000, as he said a moment ago; but he will not give to Parliament the names of the parties with whom we are going to deal. I protest most vehemently against that procedure. We have a right to know to whom this money shall go. Otherwise, we shall be compelled to believe that what is being said on the street is true; that you are making wealthier men who are already immensely wealthy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has been quite melodramatic; he has indulged in a good deal of what you might call romance. Departing from the sober discussion of facts, he mentioned street gossip and club rumour.
There is no free press; the press is chloroformed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I feel sorry for my hon. friend in his distrust of the press.
That is how the news was spread in the old days.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think a man's case is almost hopeless when he distrusts the press, because the last safeguard of liberty will be the press.
Not a gagged press, a free press.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is not
enough money in Canada to gag the Canadian press. My hon. friend is talking about a most important transaction. I usually talk to the House seriously about serious matters,and I shall answer my hon. friend' He has referred to this transaction as being a scandalous one. Let us consider for a moment the situation with which this Government is confronted. Let us go away from gossip and rumour; let us get down to facts. We have been

confronted with a great fact during the last six years, namely, the condition of certain railway systems for which the Government of which my hon. friend was a member was mainly responsible, the Grand Trunk, the National Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern Railway systems. We found the Canadian Northern Railway system, with its branches in three western provinces; with its lines through British Columbia half completed; with its line between Montreal and Port Arthur, upon which the Government of which my hon. friend was a member had given a guarantee at the rate of $35,000 a mile, a total of $35,000,000 uncompleted. We found that the Dominion Government under the Administration of which my hon. friend was a member had pledged its credit in connection with the Canadian Northern's financing. We were confronted, I say, with a grave fact, not with a theory. From time to time we have had to bring down to this House measures of assistance in order that the Canadian Northern Railway company with which was involved the credit of the Dominion, under legislation for which hon. gentlemen opposite were responsible, and with which was involved the credit of the provinces of Canada, might be enabled to complete its system and continue as a going concern. The responsibility for the Canadian Northern railway system was not upon- this Government, but the responsibility was upon us of seeing that the system was completed and continued as a solvent, going concern to serve the people. It is idle to talk of the eighteen who signed the manifesto against reciprocity. What has that to do with the Canadian Northern system?
That is what we want to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What had it to
do with the Canadian Northern system, which was jn existence long before 1911, when the manifesto was signed?

If my hon. friend will
answer our question and tell us where the stock and bonds are held, we will find out what at has to do with it. If he does not, then we will suspect what it has to do with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I was saying, we brought down from year to year legislation that was necessary to complete the system and to continue it as a going concern. Last year we announced that the 'situation had become intolerable whereby
the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific were coming to Ottawa each year for the purpose of getting further assistance. I stated that we would appoint a commission, and I indicated that in order to solve tills question permanently it might be necessary to take over one or more of the railway systems of Canada- even to nationalize the entire system of railways. This year the Canadian Northern Railway company, for reasons that have been stated a dozen times to the House during the present session, found itself in need of further aid.
We determined to take over that system in order that it might be owned and controlled by and for the people of Canada. What other way of doing it is there than the way in which we are doing it or by expropriation? We have discussed the merits of the two modes of taking over this stock- the one, by expropriation, the other, by purchase of the stock. I do not intend to discuss that now. I am simply leading up to the point at which we are at present, namely, that, in order to save this system and to save the credit of the Dominion and of the provinces, we are taking it over for the people of Canada. What is the mode of taking it over? It is this: The Dominion Government having already $40,000,000 of the stock of the company, there remains outstanding $60,000,000 of stock.
Who owns that stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Fifty per cent, of the entire issue, that is $51,000,000, is owned, as I have stated, by Mackenzie, Mann & Company, Limited. The agreement into which we are about to enter will provide that that $51,000,000 worth of stock will be deposited. Then there will be the right to the other owners and pledgees of the stock to come in and participate. If they do not do so, the Dominion Government may declare their stock to be vested in His Majesty, to be paid for at a price determined by arbitration under the provisions of this legislation. I have stated the position truly to the House. The 51 per cent of stock which, with the Dominions's 40 per cent, will give the Dominion 91 per cent, will come in at once. That leaves 9 per cent of stock. At present I do not know who are the shareholders of that 9 per cent of stock, and I do not believe that is relevant to the consideration of this question, because if the 9 per cent does not come in, the Governor in Council may declare it to be vested in His Majesty to be paid for at the price determined by arbi-

tration. If there is any information which I can get for the committee, I shall be glad to get it but, so far as I can see, the information asked for is not relevant to the consideration of this question, because we get in the 51 per cent which makes operative this agreement.
With regard to the bonds, it would not be possible for this Government, nor for any other Government, to ascertain the bondholders of the Canadian Northern Railway company. There must be tens of thousands of bondholders, principally in Great Britain. There are note-holders in the United States of America. Hon. gentlemen know that bonds and bearer notes pass from hand to hand; there is no registration of them, and the same remark can also be made with regard to stock. My hon. friend would have some difficulty in ascertaining the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway company to-day. He knows there are Shares of that company, representing hundreds of thousands of dollars of par value, standing in the names of brokers or held in vaults endorsed in blank.
Even that would be information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am giving the members of the committee the full information I have respecting this transaction. I have indicated-and I am sure it was unnecessary-why this transaction is being undertaken. It is not a question of buying stock for the sake of buying the stock. The transaction is to save this railway system as a going concern for the people of Canada, and the method we have adopted is by buying the stock. Let me ask my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who speaks about rumour and gossip connected with this transaction and who insinuates some impropriety in connection with it, would I be justified in making any insinuations in reference to the guarantee of $,'15,000,000 which the late Government gave in connection with the Canadian Northern from Montreal to Port Arthur; or with respect to the guarantees given in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific and with the contracts let on the National Transcontinental, unless I had evidence to sustain them? Would I be justified in saying that there were rumours at that time respecting those transactions? I do not believe I would. This transaction is entered into for the purpose of saving the Canadian Northern Railway system. It seems to me to be the only way in which that can be done, unless you continue to 
give aid from year to year. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) voted, in 1914, for a resolution in which his leader moved that the Dominion Government should acquire this stock by arbitration, precisely in the mode in which we are acquiring it, and he named a maximum price of $30,000,000. Supposing to-night I ask my hon. friend: Whom was he trying to help on that occasion? Would he not be justified in saying that I was unjust in my insinuations? My hon. friend is on record as having voted for that resolution. The real fact of the matter is that this talk is largely political, and my hon. friend knows that perfectly well. It is a pity, in connection with a transaction of this magnitude, undertaken for the purpose I have indicated, should be made the subject of baseless rumour and insinuation. The course my hon. friend has seen fit to adopt is not justifiable. There is nothing new about legislation brought down to assist railways in this country, the problem of transportation being as it is of the utmost importance to the community as a whole. Every year legislation of this character is brought down. Why then upon this occasion should there be any insinuations based upon what my hon. friend has termed " street rumour " or " club gossip "? I protest against the insinuations of my hon. friend. The transaction has been undertaken for the reasons I have given; it is one of the most important transactions ever before Parliament. I am always prepared to discuss seriously, before the House or in committee, any transaction for which I may be sponsor, tout my hon. friend is not fair to members of the Government when.he puts forward insinuations upon unsupported evidence. He has stated] that Sir Clifford Sifton is an owner of some of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company. I can state to my hon. friend, as I have stated before, that I have absolutely no information as to the stockholders of the Canadian Northern Railway company, with the exception that I believe Mackenzie, Mann & Company, Limited own 51 per cent of the capital stock which could be lodged so as to make this agreement operative.

I have never impugned the fair name and personal honesty of my hon. friend; I have never made any insinuations againsrt him; I believe he is acting in good faith; but I repeat this again: If he is anxious that those rumours should cease, he should do what any man of business ability-and the minister can claim

to have business ability-would do in a circumstance such as this. As he states, this is one of the greatest transactions that have come before this Parliament since Confederation. I do not believe, with the exception of t'he Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific, there has ever been a transaction of this magnitude. I ask in all fairness-are we not entitled to have at least the names of the parties who are going to benefit by this transaction? My claim is that the Canadian Northern is only a blind. We are going to pay out a large sum of money-whatever value will be attached by the arbitrators to the balance of that stock.
Besides that, we are assuming all the liabilities of the Canadian Northern company. I ask again, are not the common people of this country, whom you and I, Sir, represent, entitled to have the names of the parties who are going to benefit by this transaction? If there are no shareholders besides Mackenzie and Mann, well and good; it will be easy for us to discuss the transaction. The minister knows the secretary of the company, and with a stroke of the pen he could get this information from him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he has it.

They have a list of the shareholders and of the pledgees, and they know where the bonds are. Surely Parliament is entitled to this information. My hon. friend says that this is a big order, and complains that I am suspicious. Am I not right in being suspicious, Mr. Chairman, when I hear the Solicitor General waxing eloquent about this transaction, defending the reference to the arbitrators, and calling black to-day what he called white in 1914 on this very question. Speaking on this question in 1914 my hon. friend said (Hansard, page 3693) :
Or, if we choose, we can ourselves, by Act of Parliament, legislate that that road is the property of the people of this country and that the interests of all persons whatsoever outside of the people of Canada are eliminated.
That is what my hon. friend said in 1914.
It is quite true, too.

Perhaps my hon. friend will say whether the next sentence has the same ring of truth with it. My hon. friend had just said that we were passing this legislation to save the Canadian Northern from default, and, speaking of clause 24, he said:
The idea of that is that we are at this time making the interested parties and all stockholders parties to this contract and we say to them:	We now and here bind you that
should the day of default come you shall not appeal to the Parliament of Canada on the ground of your road being confiscated in any way whatever, but you here and now leave the Parliament of this country free from any such question and untrammelled in every way to deal with the property of the Canadian Northern as it may be advised in the interests of the people of this country. That is the summary procedure outlined here for taking over the road.
Hon. gentlemen might well drown those words in applause, because they are the condemnation of this transaction by my hon. friend. The company has gone to the wall; it cannot meet its liabilities. In 1914 we passed legislation to the effect that the moment the company went into default the axe would drop under section 24. My hon. friend gave notice to the stockholders, to Sir Clifford Sifton and others, that they could not come here and get value on that stock after the property has been confiscated. And yet, to-day, the Government come before Parliament and say: "We must save this company or the credit of Canada will be impaired." It was stated this afternoon that it would be much better to send the whole business into the hands of a receiver than to impair the credit of Canada to the extent of half a billion dollars. My hon. friend, who is quick at figures, will perhaps tell me just what the liabilities amount to per capita of our population. I have not made the calculation myself, but I ask my hon. friend was he not affrighted when he took this leap in the dark? He knows that our war debt to-day is over one billion dollars, and before the war is over it will be a very much larger amount. The population of this country is seven million or a little more, and yet my hon. friend comes before Parliament and coolly says that we must give the company more compensation. It is true that they are in default. It is true they have built their system with the public moneys of Canada and of the various provinces. It is true that we have ladled them out tons of silver and gold. Notwithstanding all that, during this terrible war, when the essential thing for Canada is to maintain unimpaired her credit in the financial markets of the world, my hon. friend says: "Yes, I have considered all that, and I now come before Parliament and insist that the Canadian Northern be satisfied." You may say what you like, Mr. Chairman, but I say that this is a scandalous transaction, and we should be given the names of those who are to benefit by it. The public have no voice in this matter, the press being absolutely silent, because it has been silenced, as it happens.
460G

unfortunately, in many democracies. It was silenced in New York by the ring that ran New York for so many years, and who, by the way, ended up in Sing Sing. It was silenced in San Francisco until the citizens took the law into their own hands. It was silenced in Chicago a few years ago when a few men were directing the municipal government of that great city, but the day came when a few honest voices were heard, and then the boodlers disappeared and public opinion came into its own.
In conclusion, I want to ask any of those hon. gentlemen who drowned in applause the words of the Solicitor General which I quoted a moment ago, whether they have seriously considered this question. Have they consulted their electors about it, and has it their approval? Were they ever authorized by their electors to countenance this legislation? I will not be stampeded by any one. I represent the farmers of the county of Eouville. I represent the people of this country.
Quebec.
Shame.

Do not blame him. He wants to get a senatorship. The hon. gentleman will shortly be one of the C.O.D. senators. So we can well understand why he stands so firmly, not for the people of this country, but for Mackenzie and Mann, the masters of this Administration.
It must be a very great solace to the heart of the 'hon. member for Rouville (iMr. Lemieux) to get off one or two of these orations occasionally.
I am not a megaphone.

Did you, Mr. Chairman, ever see so fine a spectacle of the form', trappings 'and the suits of oratory without the substance at all? The hon. gentleman has at last reached that pitiable state of mental hopelessness where he is in the condition ascribed by Macaulay to Southey of being able to believe without reason and to hate without provocation. He also seems to have albundant- time for standing around street comers and listening to gossip, or slitting around the club, hearing something there, and retailing it before this Parliament, which, I must say, has much better to do 'than listen to street comer gossip.
" The masters of the Administration," because we offer, because we propose, to take from' fhetm their stock and pay its value arbitrated by a competent tribunal. Who were the masters of the Opposition in 1914, when the very same thing was proposed? 
Who was the master of the hon. member for Rouville when he wanted us, in 1914, to take the same stock for $30,000,000 at a maximum, and pay it to the very same men? Before he voted for that resolution, in 1914, why did he not stand in his might, and majesty, and grace, and demand that we know to whom that $30,000,000 was going? Why did he not ask the leader of the Opposition, whom he was following, to take care that this money did not get into tainted hands? Will he answer? Was he chloroformed then, as he says the press is chloroformed to-day? Ah, the chloroformed press ! What is the press that is chloroformed? Is the press to be described as chloroformed because it cannot follow the vaccillating, deviating, methods of hon. gentlemen opposite? How can it follow those hon. gentlemen now, if it followed them three years ago? Is the press expected' to turn, because hon. gentlemen turn their hacks on their representations? What is the chloroformed press? Is the Toronto Star chloroformed by Mackenzie-Mann money? Is that the insinuation? The Toronto Star approves of this transaction, and approves of this policy. Why does not the hon. gentleman answer? Is- the Toronto Globe chloroformed by the money ^^'Mackenzie and Mann? The Toronto Globe will thank the hon. gentleman for his insinuation. After to-night, the last man to mention insinuation in this House should be the hon. member for Rouville-standing here and regaling us with street gossip, and then lecturing us on insinuations. I do not know who are the stockholders of the Canadian Northern, and for my part I am not interested in knowing. I would deal with those stock-holders just the same if the stock were held by the Angel Gabriel as if it were held by His Satanic Majesty?
No doubt.

It did not make any difference to the hon. gentleman in 1914 whether he had the information or not, but it has become of great importance now, because he thinks he can throw some nasty thought into the minds of the people of Canada which he does not believe for a minute himself. Never until to-night have I heard the name of Sir Clifford Sifton mentioned in connection with the stock of the Canadian Northern, I had never heard it until I heard it from the lips of the hon. member for Russell and expatiated on later by the hon. member for Rouville. I know Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, are the owners of fifty-one per cent of the stock, and I know those are the only persons with

whom we have to deal. I know that, once we make our agreement with them, the others, whoever they may be, have to take their luck on the valuation fixed by the tribunal which values the stock of Mackenzie and Mann Limited. I know nothing whatever about it, but I would be surprised if Sir Clifford Sifton owned a dollar of this stock. I am ready to give the committee not only all I know but all I have any reason to believe as being correct. Fifty-one per cent of the stock is owned by Mackenzie and Mann. Forty per cent is owned by the Dominion of Canada; that is ninety-one per cent. Only nine per cent is left. A substantial part of this nine per cent was owned in England-and I suppose is owned there yet- in respect of a certain bond issue, or more than one bond issue, which was financed or underwritten by a banking firm there. I understand this banking firm got a certain amount of stock as a bonus for the underwriting of the stock. I am not sure if I remember correctly the name of the firm, but if my recollection serves me right it is Lazards. I also understand a director of the company over there, Mr. Horne Payne, owns a portion of the stock I do not know whether that is correct or not. Then the Government of British Columbia has a substantial portion of this nine per cent, which it holds as security for certain construction work of the Canadian Northern Pacific still incomplete. I am speaking subject to correction, and only from my recollection of the information given. I understand the government of British Columbia holds about $1,500,000; in any event, it is a substantial sum. Beyond that, I have never had the slightest information, beyond that I have never made the slightest inquiry, and o uld not give the committee a particle of information more than I have given. So far as I am aware, no member of the Government has any more information, and I doubt if an'- member ever happened to get that much.
Could you not exact that information from the company?
I presume the company could give the stockholders recorded on their books.
Why don't you get it?
Because it makes no difference in the world. Why did not my hon. friend get it three years ago?
Does my hon. friend say to this House and this country that it makes no difference who the owners of the stock are?

Undoubtedly it makes no difference. We are dealing with Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, the owners of fifty-one per cent of the stock,
10 p.m. and it does not make five cents difference to the country who owns the rest of the stock.

My hon. friend says that Mackenzie and Mann are the registered owners of fitfe-sixths of the stock of the Canadian Northern railway. If he knows that, why does he not tell us who are the owners of the one-sixth?
Because I don't know.
Why should they not tell us?

It is not of any importance. whatever. If the hon. gentleman will just wait a moment, I will ask him a question. Before he voted for the same resolution in 1914, to submit the same stock to arbitration at a maximum value of $30,000,000, why did he not insist on getting the information he now seeks?

My hon. friend is
harping on that. This afternoon, for instance, he undertook to say that I moved in the House three years ago that the proposition should not be considered for six months. That is the species of casuistry my hon. friend deals in. He knows what I moved was a parliamentary motion. He knows that he and his Government voted down the motion of the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) that the whole question, should be investigated. And be knows that when this motion was voted down my proposition with regard to getting the stock was suggested simply as an alternative.

What has that to do
with the question I asked? I asked why the hon. gentleman supported an alternative- a third, or fourth, or sixth, I do not know which it was-why did he support that alternative without the very information he is demanding to-night?
Because my hon. friend had, as a member the Government, voted down a resolution moved on this side of the House, asking that the information should be given.
Not at all, there was no such resolution.

I beg my hon. friend's pardon. The resolution of the hon. member from West Middlesex was a direct

resolution asking for an investigation into the general affairs of the Company.

But, not asking an
investigation as to who owned the stock. After Parliament voted down the resolution that would have required the names of the stockholders, why did the hon. gentleman support a resolution to pay shareholders whose names he had not?

We would have
found it out had the resolution of the hon. member for West Middlesex carried.
Why did he not vote against it? What was the good of finding out who they were after the money was voted?
It was suggested to the Government. The Opposition did not pay it, the Government paid it.

The same proposal precisely, the same principle that hon. gentleman voted for on their own motion in 1914 without inquiry as to who owned the other one-ninth of the shares, they are now opposing, and they say the country cannot deal with the stock until they know who owns it. I know of no objection to getting any information as to who owns the stock. Nobody ever said he would not get the information. I contend that it is not of importance to the committee, but if the committee considers that it is, I see no objection to getting any information available. I never considered that it made the slightest difference to the country, for whom I was acting, whether the stock was owned by Tom Smith in England or John Brown in Canada. I know that Mackenzie, Mann & <10., Limited, own the greater part of the stock and I presume that this country will presume that the- people of Canada will do just as fairly by any individual in this country or any other country as by Sir William Mackenzie or Sir Donald Mann.
The hon. gentleman has said that Mackenzie, Mann & Co., Limited own 51 per cent of the stock. Will he say whether this stock or any .portion of it is pledged, and if so, with whom?

I do not know that I can say to whom it is pledged. Some is pledged to the province of British Columbia but I think the bulk is pledged to their bankers as security for various advances, which advances to a considerable extent I understand were made in respect to undertakings the primary object of which was

to bring freight to the company. I do not know the proportion, however, which can be said to be attributable to advances of that nature. The Canadian Bank of Commerce.

I have to express my personal thanks to the Solicitor General for the information which has just been extracted from him. If we had got that information earlier in the evening we would have made very substantial progress. Let me point out what has been going on in this House recently. Within the last two weeks the business of this House has on many occasions been transacted without the quorum required by the rules of Parliament. We have voted estimates without the necessary quorum. We have, indeed, enacted laws without the necessary quorum being present. Now, when a quorum is present, we are asked to pass, perhaps, as important a piece of legislation as ever came before Parliament, without having the information before us which would be insisted upon and exacted by the smallest company doing business in Canada.
Let me illustrate the .position of affairs. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), in speaking of the relations between this Government and the Canadian Northern railway, said that this Government came into power and found the Canadian Northern system. I submit that my hon. friend rather inverted the order of things-the Canadian Northern Railway system found my hon. friend and several of his colleagues and put them in power. That was the order of the happening. That having happened, let me illustrate the position of affairs. Up to that time the Minister of Finance had been the capable manager of the National Trust company. In that capacity he occupied a fiduciary position. He was, in point of fact, the trustee for those who had their investments in that company. To-day he occupies an analogous position with relation to the people of Canada. Now, while my hon. friend was manager of the National Trust company, if he had gone to a meeting of the board of directors of that company and had said: Gentlemen, here is a transaction through which I

propose to 'acquire for this company, we will say a railway, here is certain information with regard to it. If he had then been asked: With whom are we dealing, who are the beneficiaries, to whom our money is to be paid? And if my hon. friend had said: Well, I do not know these gentlemen, I do not know who they are-then I submit he would have been told to go and find out who these gentlemen were and not to come back to the board meeting until he had that information. The position is exactly analogous here. The hon. gentleman comes here in a trust capacity. He asks this committee and this Parliament to enter into a transaction, and when he is asked with whom, he says: I do not know. In effect, that is what he says, that personally he has not the information for which the Opposition asks. I for one, having had to endure the spectacle of business in this House being transacted, with regard both to estimates and to legislation, without a quorum, do not propose to sit here and take part in a transaction of this kind without registering my protest against the putting through of this legislation unless we are given the information for which we have asked, information which the Solicitor General has said, in part at least, is reasonable by virtue of the fact that he has furnished some of it himself, where this stock and where these bonds are registered. There are records, and what these records disclose should be made known to us. I agree that it may be impossible to find out at the present moment the stock holding and the bond holding, but at least we should have a knowledge of what the last registration discloses. Without that, I submit, it is improper in the highest degree to ask this committee to proceed with this legislation. I register my protest against such proceedings on the part of the Government.

I know that the Solicitor General does not wish to misrepresent any one, and so, before leaving that question of the resolution voted on in 1914, I wish to say that the resolution set forth that the whole of the stock was to be pledged with the Dominion Government for a period of five years, and if Mackenzie and Mann in that time were able to make a success of the operation, they were to be handed back the stock which was to be held in trust. Thus, at the end of five years, it would not have been necessary for the Government to find out who held the stock, because they would have held it themselves.

That was on a previous resolution moved by the bon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley).
Later on the bald resolution was proposed, seconded by the hon. gentleman from St. John, to the effect that no aid should-be given until the contract was made with the shareholders for the acquisition of the stock in a reasonable time, the value to be fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed $30,000,000.
That was in the first resolution.
Has the hon. gentleman that resolution before him?

Yes. At page 4634 of the Hansard of 1914, the resolution appears, and reads as follows:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be resolved that, under existing circumstances no assistance should be given to the Canadian Northern Railway unless at the same time it is provided that the Government have power, within a reasonable time, to acquire the ownership of the entire stock

of the company at a price to be fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed $30,000,000.

The answer to my hon. friend is that if he had voted for that resolution the country would have saved $15,000,000, because he was proposing to advance $45,000,000?

The hon. gentleman has voted to advance $60,000,000 since that resolution was moved. If he had adopted the resolution moved on this side of the House he would have saved $30,000,000.
No, the resolution said that if we had adopted that agreement we would advance $45,000,000, and would be able to get the common stock at $30,000,000 extra.

I think this co<mmittee
has something more important to deal with than what occurred three or four years ago. I submit that, whether our policy was well-judged or ill-judged has nothing to do with the responsibilities resting on the shoulders of the Government to-day. It is only fair, however, to consider the difference in the circumstances between the conditions three years ago and conditions to-day. At the time these matters were under consideration three years ago Parliament was considering the guarantee of $45,000,000 of bonds of the Canadian Northern.
I he guarantee had not been given, but was under discussion. At that time war had not broken out, and conditions were vastly different from those existing to-day, so that I do not think it is profitable, or to the point, that we should be instructed as to what one member or another member on this side of the House did three years ago, under circumstances entirely different. What was done then was done for good and sufficient reason, and what is being done to-day is being done for good and sufficient reasons, on our side of the House at any rate. Does the Government realize the difference between the conditions as they exist now, and as they were three years ago, when they gave that guarantee of $45,000? What was the debt of Canada at that time? Was it $300,000,000? What is it to-day? $1,200,000,000, or thereabouts, as I understood the Finance Min-

ister to say. Are the conditions the same in assuming a responsibility such as this, with a debt of $1,200,000,000, and the debt piling up and piling up, as it must do for an unknown period? Whether we considered wisely or not in 1914, we should consider wisely to-day where our money is going, what we are going to do with it, and where it is going to come from. If we are to meet the stupendous obligations that have piled up against us, and are piling up against us from day to day, which arise from circumstances not under our control, should we not take every care to restrict the growth of obligations that are under our control? Is that not a reason why we should most carefully consider the taking over of the vast responsibilities of the Canadian Northern railway, if that could possibly be avoided, and is it not a reason why we should consider carefully the payment of money for something that has no value? We are to buy $60,000,000 of the stock of this Canadian Northern Railway company, for what purpose? To give us control of the railway company and of the railway. We do not need to buy $60,000,000 stock of the company in order to get control of it. Mackenzie and Mann have control of the railway to-day and they have only $51,000,000 of that stock, and we could have control of the railway just as complete as Mackenzie and Mann have, if we acquired $11,000,000 of the stock. Therefore, the purchase by this Government of the difference between $11,000,000 and $60,000,000 of stock has absolutely no warrant whatever, except that it is in the nature of a hand-out to the parties concerned. Has Canada money to throw away under such circumstances? Is it confiscation to leave in the hands of whoever may happen to own it to-day $49,000,000 of the stock that they own? There is no confiscation about that.

Does the hon. gentleman think it would be fair to the people of Canada to acquire eleven per cent more, own fifty one per cent, take control, and thereby finance the company, continue to finance it, and leave in the hands of private stockholders forty-nine per cent, which stock would get the whole benefit of that financing, and ultimately become of great value?

I am not so sure that the stock will ultimately become of great value, as a result of Government operation of the road, but I am sure it will become of great value as a result of this bargain. I am satisfied the arbitration provided for

in this Act will in fact, as in intent, convey to the owners of that stock money out of the treasury of Canada out of proportion to the value of the stock as a business proposition. It will mean depletion of the treasury of Canada; it will mean injury to the credit of Canada, for the benefit of the parties interested in that stock. Now we know who is interested in the stock; it is not Mackenzie and Mann, but the Bank of Commerce. It is not a matter of rumour or of supposition that the Bank of Commerce is one of that financial group in Toronto that has a strangle hold on the progress and prosperity of this Dominion; that group to render advantage to which this Government exists and for the benefit of which the Government has shaped its legislation since it took office. To-day, for the advantage of that member of the group, it proposes to make such a raid on the Dominion treasury as never was made in the history of the Dominion.

This whole transaction from beginning to end is one that does not appeal to the people of Canada as being an honest transaction, to say nothing about its being a provident transaction. We are to be compelled to pay out of the treasury of this country sums which may amount to $60,000,000 for that which is to-day our property under the statute of 1914; and we are doing that at a time when we are passing the hat to get money to maintain the dependents of our soldiers in the field; at a time when the women of Canada are knitting socks to be provided free to our soldiers; at a time when we are implored to save and serve; at a time when we are told that we must cut out personal "extravagance of all kinds, we must restrict individual expenditure in every line, we must restrict what we eat and what we wear; at a time when we are not able to meet, as we should do, all the demands made upon us because of the exigencies of war-at that time, upwards of $60,000,000 is to be taken out of the treasury of Canada to be handed over to the Canadian Bank of Commerce in order that we may have the privilege of carrying the present obligations of the Canadian Northern Railway company and the further inestimable privilege of mismanaging the 9,500 miles of the track which that company owns-

I was surprised, coming into the House late in the evening, to hear the Solicitor General, with that superior air which he has chosen to assume towards hon. members during the last year or two since his vanity has been flattered by the Conservative press of the country, telling the committee that he did not know who -were the owners of this stock and that he had not taken the trouble to inquire. Ever since 1914, when, owing to the fact that we have in this Government a Minister of Railways who does not present to Parliament the propositions which his department fathers, the Solicitor General has been given important work to do in connection with railway matters, his vanity has been flattered by the Conservative press. Since his promotion to the Cabinet he has assumed a curious air of superiority to his fellow-members in this House. He affects an air of lackadaisical lack of interest in regard to matters. My hon. friend is the greatest sidestepper in this House. He pronounces with more assurance, whether natural or acquired, on questions of law than any judge on the bench would assume. My hon. friend is on record as to the meaning of section 24, and in the light of his challenge to me this afternoon I will read exactly what he said. After enumerating

the various guarantees the people of Canada had that the Canadian Northern would not come back for assistance, and after stating that we would control the railway for all time, he went on to say, as an alternative proposition-(Hansard p. 3693):

The idea of that is that we are at this time making the interested parties and all stockholders parties to this contract, and we say to them: We now and here bind you that should the day of default come you shall not appeal to the Parliament of Canada on the ground of your road being confiscated in any way whatever, but you here and now leave the Parliament of this country free from any such question and untrammelled in every way to deal with the property of the Canadian Northern as it may be advised in the interests of the people of this country. Oh, oh.

Does he suggest that it is in the interests of the people of Canada to provide for an arbitration board to investigate, after the Drayton-Acworth report has told us there is nothing to investigate? That is, they will own and control its stock, and the other companies will run as companies, will contract liabilities within their corporate powers, and carry on the business for which they were constituted. If the Canadian Northern requires to finance, as it does for the purpose of meeting its obligations, whether of underlying interest or otherwise, it would ask the Dominion Government to put it in funds for the purpose. The Dominion Government would make an advance to the Canadian Northern Railway company, and the Canadian Northern Railway company would ruse that advance for the purpose of paying its liabilities, whether on interest account or otherwise. The true position is that the Dominion Government is not legally liable in respect of the liabilities of the Canadian Northern or its constituent companies, but Willi continue this system, os a going concern; it is the purpose of the Dominion Government to continue this system as a going concern, and from time to time to finance it.

The stock being fully
paid up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The stock being
fully paid up. If the stock were partially paid up, there would be a liability on the unpaid stock.

It is the policy of the
Government to finance the company as a consequence of having the ownership of the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as the
interests of Canada require, the Dominion Government would from1 time to time finance the Oamadiiau Northern Railway company, in order to carry on the enterprise. That does not mean that the Canadian Northern Railway company, owned' by the Dominion Government, must at once commence extensions here, there, or the other place.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It means that it will be run having regard to the existing financial situation and the transportation needs of the people of Canada whom it serves.

I think that is entirely
satisfactory. It is understood now, that, as a consequence of this transaction the financing-that is the carrying on of the Canadian Northern railway-will in fact be a charge upon the treasury of Canada ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not put it that way. I will tell you why: because it is in the discretion of the Dominion Government to make advances, or to withhold advances, and to decide as to the amount of advances; in other words, we own the stock, and it is for the Dominion Government to determine to what extent it will finance the Canadian Northern Railway system. But it is the intention that the Canadian Northern Railway system [DOT]shall continue to be operated, in the interests of the people of Canada.

The Finance Minister,
as holder of the stock, will ask the Finance Minister of Canada if he will advance him some money to carry on the undertaking ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He will ask the Government.

It resolves itself into
one and the same thing, with the entity of the Canadian Northern remaining intact.

I should like to know from my hon. friend concerning the implementing legislation, which it is contemplated to bring down in a few days as was stated the other day by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, as regards the Quebec .and Saguenay railway, which has for its object to pay the same group of gentlemen who are interested in the Canadian Northern. I am informed the same group of financiers are the bondholders of the Quebec and Saguenay and the Quebec and Montmorency. I am told they are creditors to the amount of $3,000,000 worth of bonds, and that the contemplated legislation has for its object the payment of those bondholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information as to the bondholders or where the bonds are held, nor have I had the legislation to which he refers before me. I have been engaged with other matters.
Will the hon. minister endeavour to give to the House a statement as to the registered stockholders of the Canadian Northern?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not believe it would be possible to obtain it for tomorrow. I think we shall have to: do some cabling to get it.
If five-sixths of the stock is held by one group of people, and one-sixth held by others, a telegram to Toronto would get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would obtain the information as to the local register. I am not sure as to the other.

When procuring that information, will the hon. minister obtain information as to who holds the stock of the affiliated companies? If I understand the statement submitted to the House, there is about $6,000,000 of the stock of the affiliated companies held by people outside Mackenzie and Mann Limited, and it would be important to know also who the people are who hold that $6,000,000 stock of the affiliated companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will try to get that information but it would be quite impossible to get it by to-morrow.
Progress reported.
